userStories.title: Storage buckets and their policies exist in no applied migration, and three bucket names disagree
userStories.description: The applied schema contains zero storage.buckets rows and zero storage.objects policies. Bucket creation lives only in supabase/migrations/archive/20251031000006_create_storage_buckets.sql, which is deliberately not applied — the same US-060 squash casualty as US-068. Every access rule for uploaded avatars, listing photos and brokerage logos is therefore configured out of band: unversioned, unreviewable and invisible to verify:schema, and a fresh environment has no buckets at all. It also left three different names in use for listing photos: useListingImageUpload.ts:85 uses 'listings', OnboardingWizardPage.tsx:117 uses 'listing-images', and the archived migration defines 'listing-photos'. The object layouts disagree too — useAvatarUpload.ts writes ${user.id}/avatar.ext (first folder = uid, which is what an owner-scoped policy checks) while OnboardingWizardPage.tsx:64 writes avatars/${user.id}-${ts}.ext (first folder = the literal string 'avatars'), so an owner-scoped policy rejects the onboarding upload. Both onboarding failures are swallowed — the avatar in a catch commented 'Continue even if avatar upload fails', the listing photo behind a bare if (!uploadError) with no else.
acceptanceCriteria: A migration creates every bucket the code references, with file_size_limit and allowed_mime_types set
One bucket name for listing photos, used by every call site
Owner-scoped storage.objects policies exist for insert/update/delete, keyed on (storage.foldername(name))[1] = auth.uid()::text, with public read only where the bucket is public
Every upload path writes an object layout those policies accept — verified by executing an upload as a non-owner and seeing it rejected, and as the owner and seeing it succeed
The onboarding avatar and first-listing photo uploads surface their failures instead of swallowing them
verify:schema fails when a bucket named in a storage.from('…') call has no migration creating it (see US-089)
userStories.notes: DONE 2026-08-08 in migration 20260808000005_storage_buckets_and_policies.sql plus the three call sites. Creates avatars (5MB), listing-photos (10MB) and brokerage-logos (2MB) with file_size_limit and allowed_mime_types, and enables RLS on storage.objects (a no-op on hosted Supabase, required on a from-scratch rebuild). Standardised on listing-photos, the archived name and so the one production most likely holds; useListingImageUpload.ts moved off "listings" and OnboardingWizardPage.tsx off "listing-images". The archived policies were NOT carried over: they scoped writes with auth.role() = 'authenticated', which lets any signed-in user update or delete any other tenant's photos. The new ones key on (storage.foldername(name))[1] = auth.uid()::text, which is why the onboarding object layout had to change too — it wrote avatars/<uid>-<ts>.ext, whose first path segment is the literal string "avatars", so an owner-scoped policy rejects it. Both onboarding upload failures were also swallowed (a catch commented "Continue even if avatar upload fails", and a bare if (!uploadError) with no else); both now log and toast. SVG was deliberately dropped from brokerage-logos, which the archived definition allowed — these buckets are public, and an SVG served from the platform's own storage origin is a script-execution surface. Verified by executing against a rebuilt Postgres: A uploads under its own folder ALLOWED; A uploading under B's folder and A using the old avatars/ layout both rejected by RLS; B deleting A's objects leaves both intact; anon reads the public buckets and cannot upload. That verification needed a second prelude fix in the same shape as US-071's: scripts/supabase-prelude.sql never granted USAGE ON SCHEMA storage or table privileges on storage.objects/buckets, so every insert failed with "permission denied for schema storage" before any policy was consulted and no storage rule was testable either way.

userStories.title: Add magic-number validation to uploads — the validator exists and is imported by nothing
userStories.description: supabase/functions/_shared/fileValidation.ts is a complete implementation — validateFileType against magic numbers, validateFileSize, sanitizeFilename, hasAllowedExtension — and zero functions import it. Uploads go straight from the browser to Storage validated only by file.type (useAvatarUpload.ts:16), the browser-declared MIME, which is trivially spoofed, into buckets that have no allowed_mime_types because they have no definition at all (US-075). A user can host arbitrary content, including SVG, on the platform's public storage domain under their own path.
acceptanceCriteria: Uploads are validated by magic number, not by the client-declared MIME type
Bucket-level allowed_mime_types and file_size_limit are set as a second layer (US-075)
Uploading a file whose bytes do not match its declared type is rejected — verified by executing it with a renamed file
SVG is either rejected or served with a Content-Disposition/Content-Type that prevents it executing as a document
_shared/fileValidation.ts has at least one real caller, or is deleted
userStories.notes: DONE 2026-08-08. Three layers, only one of which is a boundary, and the module documents which. (1) New src/lib/fileValidation.ts sniffs the magic number client-side and is wired into useAvatarUpload and useListingImageUpload — this is UX, since it can be skipped. (2) allowed_mime_types and file_size_limit on the buckets from US-075 — this is the actual enforcement point, because the browser uploads straight to Storage and never passes through a function. (3) supabase/functions/_shared/fileValidation.ts, previously imported by nothing, now has a real caller: optimize-image validates the stored bytes before handing them to ImageMagick, because feeding arbitrary input to an image decoder is the classic way an upload becomes an exploit. The client sniffer does two things a naive signature table gets wrong: WebP is checked for the WEBP tag at offset 8 and not just the RIFF container (a .wav is also RIFF), and an unrecognised MIME type fails rather than passes. 8 tests cover it, including an SVG renamed to image/png and a .wav claiming to be WebP. Writing them surfaced a real wart: the size message read "File size must be less than 0MB" for any sub-MB limit, now formatted in KB below 1MB.

userStories.title: Unauthenticated SSRF in seven URL-fetching edge functions
userStories.description: crawl-site, check-broken-links, check-security-headers, detect-redirect-chains, analyze-images, check-core-web-vitals and check-mobile-first all take a caller-supplied URL, pass it through new URL() — which parses, it does not validate — and fetch it. No scheme check, no private-range or link-local block, no allow-list. http://169.254.169.254/ and http://127.0.0.1:<port>/ are both reachable, from a process holding the service-role key, with the response body returned to the caller. _shared/url-validation.ts exists but only covers redirect URLs for SSO; there is no SSRF guard in the codebase. All seven are also unauthenticated (US-078).
acceptanceCriteria: A shared guard in _shared/ rejects any URL that is not http/https, resolves to a private, loopback, link-local or unique-local address, or names a metadata endpoint
The guard resolves DNS and checks the resolved address, so a hostname pointing at 127.0.0.1 is rejected too
All seven functions call it before any fetch, including on redirect hops (detect-redirect-chains follows Location headers)
Requests for 169.254.169.254, 127.0.0.1, 10.0.0.0/8 and a public hostname with a private A record are all rejected — verified by executing the functions
A legitimate public URL still crawls successfully
userStories.notes: DONE 2026-08-08. New supabase/functions/_shared/ssrf-guard.ts, wired into all seven. safeFetch() replaces bare fetch() in crawl-site, check-broken-links, check-security-headers, detect-redirect-chains, analyze-images and check-mobile-first; check-core-web-vitals hands the URL to Google's PageSpeed API rather than fetching it, so it validates the input instead — a private address there cannot reach our network but is still a request we should not make on someone's behalf, and it leaks internal hostnames to a third party. The guard blocks non-http(s) schemes, localhost/.internal, and the private, loopback, link-local, CGNAT, multicast and reserved ranges — and, importantly, RESOLVES the hostname and checks the answer, because internal.example.com with an A record of 10.0.0.5 defeats any string check. It re-checks every redirect hop, since a public URL that 302s to 127.0.0.1 defeats a single up-front check. One subtlety found while wiring it: detect-redirect-chains passes redirect: manual and walks the chain itself to report every hop, and safeFetch following redirects internally would have consumed exactly what that function exists to show — safeFetch now honours an explicit manual redirect, guarding the URL and returning the single response, with per-hop safety preserved because the caller comes back through it. 6 tests cover the address matching, including IPv4-mapped IPv6 (::ffff:127.0.0.1) and the ranges either side of the private blocks (172.15/172.32, 192.167/192.169) so an over-broad prefix check would fail. Running them needed vitest.config.ts extended to include supabase/functions/**/*.test.ts — CI only ran deno check over that tree, which type-checks but executes nothing, so pure logic there had no test at all. RESIDUAL, NOT CLOSED: DNS rebinding. The name is resolved here and again by fetch(), and a hostile resolver can answer differently; closing it needs connect-time pinning that Deno's fetch does not expose.

userStories.title: Service-role edge functions with no authorization at all
userStories.description: apply-seo-autofix builds a service-role client and acts on the request body with no requireAuth, no requireAdmin and no signature check. It is not declared in config.toml, and verify_jwt = true would not help: the anon key is itself a valid project JWT, so verify_jwt distinguishes 'has the public key' from 'has no key', not 'is an admin'. Same shape: schedule-seo-audit, test-social-webhook, test-ai-model, monitor-performance-budget, and the AI-spend endpoints generate-blog-content, generate-content-suggestions and generate-social-post. notify-lead too — anyone can POST a lead_id or a forged record and drive email sends.
acceptanceCriteria: Every function that builds a service-role client requires either requireAdmin, requireAuth with an ownership check, or isServiceRoleRequest — matching what the function actually does
notify-lead accepts only service-role callers (it is invoked by a database trigger), and ignores a caller-supplied record in favour of looking the lead up by id
Calling each of the listed functions with only the anon key returns 401 or 403 — verified by executing them
The legitimate callers (the SEO admin UI, the pg_net triggers, the schedulers) still work
config.toml declares every function on disk, so nothing depends on the CLI default
userStories.notes: DONE 2026-08-08. Every function building a service-role client now carries a guard matching what it does. requireAdmin on the admin-grade set: apply-seo-autofix, schedule-seo-audit, test-social-webhook, test-ai-model, monitor-performance-budget, health-check, the three AI-spend generators (generate-blog-content, generate-content-suggestions, generate-social-post) and the eleven SEO crawlers. isServiceRoleRequest on the scheduled jobs (send-scheduled-bio-emails, send-scheduled-listing-emails) and on notify-lead, which is invoked by the leads-INSERT trigger via pg_net. notify-lead additionally stopped trusting payload.record: it now takes only the id and re-reads the lead from the database, because accepting the record verbatim let an unauthenticated caller drive an email with contents of their choosing. The eleven genuinely public functions stay public and are rate limited instead: generate-listing-description and send-listing-generator-email gained the DB-backed limiter, and send-bio-analyzer-email was migrated off _shared/rateLimit.ts — a module-level Map, useless across ephemeral isolates — which required hoisting its client above the check. generate-sitemap, login-security, oauth-proxy, sso-initiate, sso-callback and rate-limit remain unlimited by design (login-security and rate-limit ARE the limiters; the SSO flows need care that belongs in their own story). NOTE the framing that made this necessary: verify_jwt = true would not have helped any of these, because the anon key is itself a valid project JWT — it separates "has the public key" from "has no key", not "is an admin". Four of the five _shared/rateLimit.ts consumers remain, all Stripe; US-084 owns deleting it.

userStories.title: The brute-force lockout can never fire — the 429 is swallowed by the fail-open path
userStories.description: login-security signals a block with HTTP 429. callEdgeFunction throws on any non-2xx (src/lib/edgeFunctions.ts:63), so edgeFunctions.invoke returns { data: null, error }, and checkLoginThrottle's fail-open branch (useLoginSecurity.ts:39-49) returns blocked: false, attemptsRemaining: 5. The one response the throttle exists to produce is the one it discards, and Login.tsx:96's if (throttleResult.blocked) is unreachable. tests/security/auth.security.spec.ts:40 — 'should implement login rate limiting' — targets exactly this and is never run by CI (US-088).
acceptanceCriteria: A blocked account is actually blocked at the UI — either login-security returns 200 with blocked: true in the body, or callEdgeFunction passes 429 bodies through
Six failed logins in the throttle window produce the lockout message rather than a sixth password prompt — verified by executing it
A genuine network failure still fails open rather than locking everyone out
tests/security/auth.security.spec.ts's rate-limiting spec passes
npm run test:run still passes
userStories.notes: DONE 2026-08-08. login-security now answers the throttle check with HTTP 200 and the verdict in the body, keeping Retry-After as a header when blocked. It previously answered 429, and callEdgeFunction throws on any non-2xx, so edgeFunctions.invoke returned { data: null, error } and checkLoginThrottle's fail-open branch converted the block into blocked: false — the one verdict the throttle exists to produce was the one it discarded, and Login.tsx:96's `if (throttleResult.blocked)` was unreachable. A throttle verdict is a successful answer about state, not a transport failure. The fail-open branch itself is deliberately kept for genuine transport failures: a throttle that cannot be reached must not lock every user out. Added src/hooks/useLoginSecurity.test.ts with four cases covering the contract in both directions — a block is reported, the email is normalised before the call, and both an { error } result and a thrown call still fail open. That test suite caught a trap worth recording: `beforeEach(() => invoke.mockReset())` returns the mock function, and vitest treats a function returned from a hook as a teardown callback, so it CALLED the mock after each test and the throwing implementation surfaced as an unhandled rejection that failed the run. A block body fixes it. NOT CLOSED BY THIS STORY: the control is client-side, so an attacker posting straight to GoTrue's /token endpoint never touches it. The real limit belongs at the gateway; treat this as UX. The Playwright spec that covers this (tests/security/auth.security.spec.ts:40) still does not run in CI — that is US-090.

userStories.title: Enforce plan limits server-side — they are currently advisory
userStories.description: useSubscriptionLimits.canAdd() gates the UI only. check_subscription_limit and check_feature_limit exist in the database but no trigger and no RLS policy calls either — verified: no trigger function matching %limit% on any table. The only constraint on listings, links and testimonials is auth.uid() = user_id, so a free-plan user (3 listings) can POST directly to /rest/v1/listings and create unlimited rows. Every plan tier is advisory.
acceptanceCriteria: A BEFORE INSERT trigger on listings, links and testimonials calls check_subscription_limit and raises when the plan limit is reached
A free-plan user creating a 4th listing via a direct PostgREST call is rejected — verified by executing it, not through the UI
A user with no subscriptions row is treated as free rather than unlimited
-1 continues to mean unlimited
The client-side check stays as UX and its message matches what the server enforces
npm run verify:schema passes
userStories.notes: DONE 2026-08-08 in migration 20260808000007_enforce_plan_limits.sql. BEFORE INSERT triggers on listings, links and testimonials. check_subscription_limit() was NOT reused as the enforcement point because it gets two cases wrong, both of which would have been worse than no enforcement: -1 means unlimited everywhere else in the product, but `count < -1` is false, so it blocked every insert on an unlimited plan; and with no subscriptions row max_allowed is NULL and `count < NULL` is NULL, not false, so a naive guard failed open. It is fixed here as well (-1 short-circuits to true, a missing row falls back to the free tier) and a dedicated enforce_plan_limit() trigger function raises check_violation with a hint. Deliberate exemption: only owner-initiated inserts are metered (auth.uid() = NEW.user_id). An anonymous visitor submitting a review under US-074 or a lead has no way to know or influence the agent's plan, and silently dropping someone's review because the agent is at their tier is a worse failure than the overage; service-role writes are exempt for the same reason. Verified as a free-plan user against a rebuilt Postgres: listings 1, 2 and 3 created, the 4th rejected by enforce_plan_limit, and an anonymous testimonial for that same at-limit user still accepted.

userStories.title: Extend verify:schema with column-level and structural checks
userStories.description: verify:schema confirms every table referenced in code exists but not every column, which is the exact blind spot that let US-070 (profiles.email in five functions) and US-083 (the sitemap's columns) ship. The six checks below each catch a defect found in the 2026-08 review, and the first alone catches six sites across four subsystems.
acceptanceCriteria: Every column named in a .select('…') list in src/ and supabase/functions/ exists on the target table, with embedded-resource syntax (foo:bar(...), rel!inner(...)) handled
Every trigger function defined in public is attached to at least one table
No view granted to anon or authenticated lacks security_invoker
No RLS policy reachable by anon exposes a column matching *secret*, *token*, *_key, *webhook_url or *certificate
Every bucket named in a storage.from('…') call is created by a migration
No RLS policy references auth.users directly
Each new check fails on the pre-fix tree and passes on the post-fix tree — demonstrated, not asserted
npm run verify:schema passes
userStories.notes: DONE 2026-08-08 in scripts/verify-schema.mjs, which now runs 12 checks instead of 8. Five of the six criteria are implemented; the sixth (no policy references auth.users directly) was already satisfied by US-088 and is covered by check 3 plus the new check 12, so no separate check was added. NEW CHECK 9 — every column named in a .select() exists on the target table. This is the one that matters: check 4 proved the TABLE existed and nothing proved the COLUMNS did, which is exactly how five edge functions shipped selecting profiles.email. It handles the PostgREST select grammar — embedded resources profiles(username) and profiles!inner(...), aliases alias:column, JSON paths col->>key, casts col::text, aggregates — and skips select(*) and the generated types.ts. It immediately found one live defect nobody had filed separately: src/pages/admin/HealthDashboard.tsx selecting user_subscriptions.plan_name, a column on the flat subscriptions table rather than the relational one, wrapped in a catch that swallowed the 400 so the revenue widget rendered empty forever. Fixed in the same commit and now reads subscriptions, with the error logged instead of swallowed. NEW CHECK 10 — every trigger function in public is attached to something (catches US-068; check 1 happily validated the orphaned handle_new_user). NEW CHECK 11 — no view granted to anon/authenticated lacks security_invoker (catches US-071). NEW CHECK 12 — no secret-shaped column is reachable by anon. The first draft of 12 was wrong and reported 51 findings: it read information_schema.column_privileges alone, which just reflects Supabase's blanket GRANT ALL to anon and says nothing about reachability. Rewritten to require BOTH the column privilege AND a SELECT policy anon can actually satisfy — one whose qualifier does not reference auth.uid(), has_role(), auth.role() or auth.jwt() — which is precisely the shape of the two real defects (is_published = true, active = true) and matches nothing else. NEW NOTE 13 — buckets referenced by storage.from() that no migration creates; a note rather than a check until US-075 lands, at which point flip it to check(). Every new check was demonstrated to fire by reintroducing the original defect against the live database and watching it fail, then restoring: dropping on_auth_user_created fires 10; resetting security_invoker on user_subscription_details and re-granting to anon fires 11; recreating the SSO policy fires 12 with 2 findings; re-granting zapier_webhook_url to anon fires 12 with 1. All 12 green afterwards.

userStories.title: The sitemap silently omits every article and every listing
userStories.description: generate-sitemap selects articles.featured_image (the real column is featured_image_url) and listings.title, images (the real columns are address and photos). The generated sitemap contains an entry per published article and per active listing on a published profile — verified by generating it against seeded data
A query error fails the request or is surfaced, rather than silently emitting a partial sitemap

userStories.title: Stripe hardening: real rate limiting, durable idempotency, and a fail-closed plan default
userStories.description: Three defects in the billing path. (1) There are two rate limiters: _shared/rate-limiter.ts is DB-backed via rpc('check_rate_limit'), _shared/rateLimit.ts is a module-level Map — useless across ephemeral horizontally-scaled isolates — and the in-memory one is the one guarding create-checkout-session, create-portal-session, create-stripe-customer and report-stripe-usage. (2) stripe-webhook keeps processed event IDs in a module-level Map, so Stripe's retries land on cold instances and reprocess; the module-scope setInterval also pins the isolate for no benefit. (3) getPlanNameFromPriceId ends `return priceMap[priceId] || 'professional'` and the result feeds getPlanLimits, so any price ID not in the hardcoded map or the STRIPE_PRICE_* env vars silently grants professional entitlements.
acceptanceCriteria: The four Stripe functions use the DB-backed limiter and _shared/rateLimit.ts is deleted
Webhook idempotency is persisted in a table keyed on the Stripe event id, with the unique violation as the check
Replaying the same webhook event twice against a cold instance processes it once — verified by executing it
An unrecognised price ID resolves to 'free', not 'professional', and is logged as an error
The module-scope setInterval is removed
npm run verify:schema passes
userStories.notes: DONE 2026-08-08 in migration 20260808000009_stripe_webhook_idempotency.sql plus the five functions. (1) All four Stripe endpoints moved off _shared/rateLimit.ts onto the DB-backed checkRateLimitDb, and rateLimit.ts is deleted — it was a module-level Map, so it reset on every cold start and never saw a sibling isolate's counts, meaning the money endpoints had the one limiter in the codebase that did not work. rate-limiter.ts gained a getRateLimitHeaders matching the old helper so the swap did not change any response shape. (2) Webhook idempotency is now a stripe_processed_events table with the event id as primary key, and the unique constraint IS the check — an insert that conflicts means the event is already handled, which is race-free in a way the old read-then-write Map was not even in principle. The claim fails OPEN on any error other than 23505: Stripe retries, and processing an event twice is far less damaging than dropping a subscription change. The module-scope setInterval sweeper is gone with it. (3) getPlanNameFromPriceId ended `|| 'professional'`, so any price id not in the hardcoded map or the STRIPE_PRICE_* env vars — a new tier, an add-on, a typo — silently granted professional entitlements. It now falls back to 'free' and logs the unrecognised id as an error; entitlement defaults fail closed. Verified against a rebuilt Postgres: the first claim inserts, a replay is rejected with 23505, one row remains. RECORDED, NOT FIXED: billing state is still split across subscriptions (flat, with the limit columns, read by useSubscriptionLimits) and user_subscriptions (relational, read by checkout/portal). stripe-webhook dual-writes both consistently across all five event types so it works today, but two sources of truth kept in sync by one function is a standing hazard and deserves its own story.

userStories.title: Adopt native Supabase MFA so the second factor is enforced in the token, not the client
userStories.description: signInWithPassword completes and issues a full session before any second factor is considered (useAuthStore.ts:318-377). requiresMFA is ordinary Zustand state and MFAChallenge sets mfaVerified on success, so someone with the password and no TOTP already holds a working access_token: they can call PostgREST directly, or run useAuthStore.setState({ mfaVerified: true }). Separately SecureRoute's requireMFA prop is a no-op because getSecurityContext hardcodes isMFAVerified = true (authentication.ts:196-207, comment: 'For now, assume verified if they got past login').
acceptanceCriteria: MFA uses Supabase's native enrol/challenge/verify so that the second factor determines the session's AAL
A user with MFA enabled who has not completed the challenge cannot read their own leads via a direct PostgREST call — verified by executing it with the pre-challenge token
RLS on at least the lead and subscription tables requires aal2 for MFA-enrolled users
getSecurityContext reports real MFA state rather than a hardcoded true, and SecureRoute's requireMFA prop does something
Existing enrolled users are migrated or re-enrolled without being locked out
npm run test:run still passes
userStories.notes:
IN PROGRESS 2026-09-01. Client-side native MFA is implemented; the RLS enforcement is written but DELIBERATELY NOT APPLIED. Scope was agreed with the user: implement the flow, hold back the part that can lock people out until it can be verified against a real GoTrue.

WHAT IS DONE:
- src/hooks/useNativeMFA.ts: enrol / challenge / verify / unenroll through supabase.auth.mfa, plus a status read from getAuthenticatorAssuranceLevel() + listFactors() so the client's view of MFA comes from the token rather than from local state.
- useAuthStore.signIn: requiresMFA now derives from the token's AAL (nextLevel === 'aal2' && currentLevel === 'aal1'), not from a user_mfa_settings boolean. The flags drive ROUTING only — setState({mfaVerified:true}) no longer buys access to anything once the RLS below is applied.
- getSecurityContext (lib/security/authentication.ts): the hardcoded `isMFAVerified = true` with its 'For now, assume verified if they got past login' comment is gone. It reads the real AAL, and on any error it fails CLOSED rather than defaulting to verified. SecureRoute's requireMFA prop consumes this and therefore does something now.
- NativeMFAVerification / NativeMFASettings components, wired into /auth/mfa and dashboard Settings.

EXISTING ENROLLED USERS — the migration path, which the notes asked to be planned first. The old TOTP secret CANNOT be transplanted: it is encrypted with PII_ENCRYPTION_KEY inside the Edge Function, and Supabase has no supported write path into auth.mfa_factors other than mfa.enroll(), which mints its own secret. So re-enrolment is unavoidable. It is authorised by the OLD factor (useNativeMFA.migrateLegacyFactor): the user enters their current code, it is checked through the legacy verify-mfa function, and only then is the native factor enrolled and the legacy row disabled. A password alone can never enrol a replacement. Nobody is locked out, and both systems are live only for the length of each user's own transition.

NOT DONE — and this is the half that provides the actual protection:
supabase/migrations/pending/20260901000002_require_aal2_for_mfa_users.sql adds a mfa_satisfied() predicate to the SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE policies on leads and to SELECT on subscriptions/user_subscriptions. It is in pending/ because supabase/migrations/*.sql is a non-recursive glob, so neither CI nor `supabase db push` picks it up. Applying it BEFORE the client changes ship and users have re-enrolled locks out every enrolled agent, since nothing will have upgraded their session to aal2. The preconditions and the query for counting un-migrated users are in supabase/migrations/pending/README.md.

LEGACY UI REMOVED: useMFA, MFASetup, MFASettings and MFAVerification are deleted. Once the native flow landed nothing referenced them — they formed a closed island pointing at the old backend — and keeping them would have left two MFA UIs live against two systems, which is what this story's note warns against. Only the Edge Functions remain: setup-mfa is now unused, and verify-mfa / disable-mfa are still called by the re-enrolment bridge. Retire all three, plus user_mfa_settings / mfa_temp_codes / mfa_trusted_devices / mfa_verification_logs, once the enrolled count above reaches zero.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA STATUS:
1. Native enrol/challenge/verify determines AAL — DONE (code), UNVERIFIED (no GoTrue available locally).
2. Pre-challenge token cannot read own leads via direct PostgREST — NOT MET. Requires the pending migration, and needs executing with a real pre-challenge token to prove.
3. RLS on lead and subscription tables requires aal2 — WRITTEN, NOT APPLIED.
4. getSecurityContext reports real MFA state and requireMFA does something — DONE.
5. Existing users migrated without lockout — DESIGNED AND IMPLEMENTED, UNVERIFIED.
6. npm run test:run passes — DONE (304 passed; tsc 0 errors, build passes, verify:schema passes).

TESTS: src/lib/security/mfa-assurance.test.ts covers every branch of how isMFAVerified is derived — no factor, enrolled-but-unchallenged, enrolled-and-challenged, legacy enrolment, and the error path. That last one matters most: the old code defaulted to VERIFIED on any error, and 'fails closed' is a claim worth holding to a test. The enrol/challenge round trip itself is still uncovered — it needs a real GoTrue.

NEXT STEP for whoever picks this up: stand up a staging Supabase, exercise enrol -> sign out -> sign in -> challenge, confirm the JWT carries aal2, then execute criterion 2 explicitly with a captured pre-challenge token before promoting the pending migration.

userStories.title: PII encryption on leads is defence-in-depth theatre
userStories.description: leads.encrypted_email and encrypted_phone are dual-written by useLeads.ts:78, but the plaintext email and phone columns are still populated on the same row under the same RLS, so the ciphertext protects nothing an attacker could not already read. submit-lead — the path every public capture should use — writes no encrypted columns at all, so coverage is inconsistent as well as ineffective. gdpr-export/index.ts:174 already carries a TODO to decrypt on read.
acceptanceCriteria: Either the plaintext columns are dropped and every reader decrypts (useLeads already has the read path), or the encrypted columns are dropped and the feature stops being described as encryption at rest
Whichever direction is chosen is applied consistently across useLeads, submit-lead and gdpr-export
Existing rows are backfilled or migrated, not left in a mixed state
gdpr-export returns readable contact details for the data subject
npm run verify:schema passes
userStories.notes:
DONE 2026-09-01. Chose the option the story names as the only real one: the plaintext leads.email/leads.phone columns are dropped and every reader decrypts.

The cost objection in the original note ('every query that filters or sorts on email/phone has to change, and search over encrypted columns is not free') turned out not to apply. Nothing filters or sorts on those columns in SQL: there is no .ilike/.eq against leads.email or leads.phone anywhere in src/ or supabase/functions/, and the one lead search (dashboard/Leads.tsx) runs client-side over rows useLeads has already decrypted. So the honest option was also the cheap one.

Applied consistently across all four paths the story names:
- useLeads: encrypted-only on insert and update (was dual-writing); read path already decrypted.
- submit-lead: now encrypts before insert. This was the real coverage hole — the path every public capture form uses wrote NO ciphertext at all.
- gdpr-export: now decrypts for the subject's own copy, closing the TODO at index.ts:174. A subject access request that returned ciphertext would not be an export.
- sample-data-service: now encrypts.
- useSecureLeads: deleted. It had no callers and never decrypted, so reviving it would have shown ciphertext in the UI.
- useAnalytics: selects encrypted_* and decrypts, because LeadsTable renders email and phone.

MIGRATION SAFETY. The AES key lives only in the Edge Function secrets (US-066), so no SQL can encrypt and the backfill has to be a function: supabase/functions/backfill-lead-pii (admin-only, idempotent, batched). 20260901000001_leads_drop_plaintext_pii.sql counts rows that still hold plaintext with no ciphertext and RAISES rather than dropping. Verified both branches against a real Postgres: with an un-backfilled row it refuses and the email survives; after backfill it drops cleanly. Order is documented in DEPLOYMENT.md §2.2.

OPERATIONAL RISK, stated plainly in DEPLOYMENT.md: PII_ENCRYPTION_KEY is now the ONLY way to read a lead's contact details. There is no plaintext column to reconstruct from any more, which also means key rotation must decrypt under the old key first. The previous §2.1 text said retiring these columns should wait until after any rotation for exactly that reason; that trade is now made deliberately and written down rather than left implicit.

VERIFIED: npm run verify:schema passes (all 12 checks — it caught three real integration points during this work: the check's own insert, useAnalytics' select, and the backfill's pre-drop read). types.ts regenerated from the migrated schema and `types:check` reports it in sync. npx tsc --noEmit 0 errors. npm run test:run 298 passed. npm run build passes.

NOT VERIFIED: nothing here has run against the live database. The backfill function has not been executed, and the migration has only been applied to a local Postgres built from supabase/migrations. Run the DEPLOYMENT.md §2.2 sequence in a staging environment before production.

NOTE for whoever picks up US-085: deriving Lead from the row surfaced the same class of defect US-056 kept finding — leads.created_at and leads.status are nullable, and Leads.tsx treated an undated lead as breaching the SLA (new Date(null) is the epoch), while useMLLeadScoring put it at hour 0 on a Thursday and skewed its time-of-day features. Both fixed here.

Every trend arrow on /dashboard/analytics-advanced therefore reads a constant +17.6% regardless of what happened, including during a decline. revenue and avgResponseTime are hardcoded 0 in the same object and flow into the KPI cards.

A period with fewer views than the one before it renders a negative trend
revenue and avgResponseTime are either computed or removed from the KPI cards rather than displayed as 0

userStories.notes: DONE 2026-08-08. useAnalytics now queries the preceding window of the same length and returns previousStats, replacing AnalyticsDashboard's `Math.round(stats.totalViews * 0.85)` with the comment "Estimate 15% growth" — which made every trend arrow read a constant +17.6% regardless of what happened, including during a decline, when it showed growth. userStories.title: Fix the keywords admin policies — they error for everyone, including admins
userStories.description: The three keywords write policies use EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM auth.users WHERE users.id = auth.uid() AND users.raw_user_meta_data->>'role' = 'admin'). Policies are evaluated with the caller's privileges and authenticated has no grant on auth.users, so the check raises — verified: ERROR: permission denied for table users. Keyword management is therefore broken for admins too. Separately, raw_user_meta_data is user-writable via auth.updateUser({ data: … }), so if that grant ever appeared any user could self-declare role: admin.
acceptanceCriteria: The three policies use has_role(auth.uid(), 'admin'::app_role) like the other 270-odd policies
An admin can insert, update and delete keywords — verified by executing it as an admin
A non-admin cannot, and a non-admin who sets raw_user_meta_data.role = 'admin' still cannot
No RLS policy in the public schema references auth.users directly (see US-082)
npm run verify:schema passes
userStories.notes: DONE 2026-08-08 in migration 20260808000003_fix_keywords_admin_policies.sql. The three write policies now use has_role(auth.uid(), 'admin'::app_role) TO authenticated, matching the ~270 other policies. Verified on a rebuilt Postgres: an admin can insert, update and delete; a non-admin is rejected with "new row violates row-level security policy" on insert, and their UPDATE and DELETE affect 0 rows. The non-admin used in the test has raw_user_meta_data set to {"role":"admin"} — the exact escalation the old policy would have permitted had the auth.users grant ever existed — and is still denied. anon still reads active keywords. Worth recording how nearly this was mis-verified: the first test run reported "UNEXPECTEDLY ALLOWED" for the non-admin insert, which was an artefact of psql continuing past a failed statement without ON_ERROR_STOP and printing the trailing SELECT anyway. The same trap produced a false "SELF-GRANT SUCCEEDED" during the original review. Always set ON_ERROR_STOP when a test asserts that something is denied.

userStories.title: Run the 47 security specs and 5 e2e specs in CI
userStories.description: tests/security/ holds 47 Playwright specs — 14 auth, 21 headers, 12 XSS — and tests/e2e/ holds 5. ci.yml runs eslint and test:a11y and nothing else from tests/. One of the unrun specs, tests/security/auth.security.spec.ts:40 'should implement login rate limiting', targets exactly the control US-079 proves broken. The suites exist, are maintained, and produce no signal.
acceptanceCriteria: ci.yml runs npm run test:security and npm run test:e2e
The jobs have whatever Supabase environment they need, via secrets rather than a committed .env
The suites pass, or each failing spec is either fixed or explicitly skipped with a linked story — no blanket continue-on-error
A newly introduced security regression fails the build — demonstrated by temporarily reverting one fix
userStories.notes: These need a reachable Supabase and a seeded test account, which is why they were probably never wired up. A disposable project or a seeded local stack is the prerequisite; if that is out of scope, say so in the story rather than adding a job that is green because it skipped everything. CHECKED 2026-08-08, still open and here is precisely why. ci.yml does have jobs named `security` and `accessibility`, which is misleading: `security` runs `npm audit --audit-level=high` and eslint, not the 47 Playwright specs, and `accessibility` runs the single a11y spec. So tests/security/ (14 auth, 21 headers, 12 XSS) and tests/e2e/ (5) remain unrun by anything. Worth recording alongside US-091: `npm audit --audit-level=high` is blocking and NOT continue-on-error, so with 21 high advisories that job was failing on every push until this session cleared them — a second permanently-red signal nobody was reading, the same failure mode as the typecheck job in US-056. The blocker for this story is unchanged and is environmental, not code: the specs need a reachable Supabase and a seeded test account (playwright.config.ts starts `npm run dev`, which needs VITE_SUPABASE_URL/ANON_KEY, and the auth specs need credentials to log in with). Adding the job without those would produce exactly what this story warns against — a green job that skipped everything. NEXT STEP for whoever picks this up: stand up a disposable Supabase project or a seeded local stack, put the URL/key/test-account in repository secrets, then add the job modelled on the existing accessibility one (it already shows the `npx playwright install --with-deps chromium` pattern). Note that at least one spec is expected to have been failing: tests/security/auth.security.spec.ts:40 targets the login rate limiting that US-079 proved was never firing.

acceptanceCriteria: src/components/dashboard/LinkManager.tsx is deleted
The HealthDashboard subscription widget queries real columns and renders

The open anonymous INSERT stays — this is a public link-in-bio, visitors have no session, and view tracking has to work for them — but it is now bounded: a BEFORE INSERT trigger caps 30 views per minute per (visitor, profile), silently dropping over-limit rows via RETURN NULL rather than raising, since a rejected view must not surface as an error on a visitor page and the client insert is fire-and-forget. A trigger rather than an edge function because the insert goes straight from the browser to PostgREST and moving it would change the tracking path for every profile. Two mistakes worth recording. First, the trigger called check_rate_limit as though it returned a boolean; it RETURNS TABLE(allowed, remaining, reset_at), so every insert failed with "argument of NOT must be type boolean, not type record" — and the verification then read "0 recorded", which looked exactly like a working throttle. Second, after fixing that, the count still read 0 because the verification query ran as anon and analytics_views SELECT is scoped to auth.uid() = user_id — anon cannot read back what it just wrote. Re-checked as the owner: 50 forged views from one visitor -> 30 recorded, a different visitor unaffected. HONEST LIMIT: visitor_id comes from localStorage and is trivially rotated, so this raises the cost of inflation rather than preventing it. The counters should be treated as indicative.

userStories.title: Account deletion fails outright, and would orphan tenant data if it did not
userStories.description: Found while verifying US-083. process_scheduled_account_deletions() performs DELETE FROM auth.users, which raises: insert or update on table "audit_logs" violates foreign key constraint "audit_logs_actor_id_fkey". The chain is: deleting auth.users cascades to profiles (FK ON DELETE CASCADE) -> the audit_profiles_changes trigger fires -> audit_table_change calls log_audit_event with p_actor_id => auth.uid(), which is NULL under the cron/service-role caller, so log_audit_event COALESCEs it to the user being deleted -> that INSERT references an auth.users row already removed in the same statement -> FK violation -> the whole DELETE aborts. ON DELETE SET NULL on audit_logs does not help because the row is being inserted, not updated. So a GDPR right-to-erasure request is accepted, scheduled, the 30-day grace period elapses, and the job then errors forever. Separately, even once the delete succeeds it would not erase much: leads, listings, testimonials, user_settings, article_webhooks and analytics_views have no foreign key on user_id at all, so nothing cascades to them. Those rows carry lead names, emails and phone numbers.
acceptanceCriteria: DELETE FROM auth.users for a provisioned account succeeds — verified by executing it, not by reading the function
The audit trigger does not write an actor_id that no longer exists (skip the audit row on cascade-delete, or drop the FK to ON DELETE SET NULL semantics that apply at insert time)
An erased account leaves no rows in leads, listings, testimonials, user_settings, article_webhooks or analytics_views — verified by counting them after the delete
Foreign keys with ON DELETE CASCADE exist on the tenant tables that lack them, added NOT VALID first if production may hold orphans
The audit trail of the deletion itself survives the deletion (an erasure record with a null actor is fine; losing the record is not)
npm run verify:schema passes
userStories.notes: DONE 2026-08-08 in migration 20260808000006_fix_account_deletion.sql. Two defects. (1) The DELETE aborted: deleting auth.users cascades to profiles, the audit trigger fires, audit_table_change() finds auth.uid() NULL under the cron caller and falls back to the row's own id, and log_audit_event() then inserts that as user_id/actor_id — referencing an auth.users row already removed in the same statement. ON DELETE SET NULL on audit_logs does not help, because the row is being INSERTED with a dangling reference rather than updated to one. log_audit_event now nulls either id when the referenced user is gone, so the erasure RECORD survives while the reference does not — losing the audit trail of a deletion would be worse than losing the actor on it. (2) leads, listings, testimonials, user_settings, article_webhooks and analytics_views carried a user_id with no foreign key at all, so nothing cascaded to them even once the delete worked. Added ON DELETE CASCADE, NOT VALID: production may hold orphans from before this and a validating ADD CONSTRAINT would fail on them, while NOT VALID still enforces on new rows and still cascades, which is what erasure needs. Sweep orphans and VALIDATE as a follow-up. account_deletion_log deliberately gets no cascading FK — it has to outlive the user. Verified end to end on a rebuilt Postgres by seeding a user with a profile, lead, listing, testimonial, settings row and analytics row and running the exact DELETE the scheduler runs: it now succeeds (previously an FK error), every one of those counts goes to 0, and 3 audit rows survive with actor_id nulled.

The leads an agent most wants to nurture, the not-yet-approved ones, are exactly the ones lost. All four pre-approval answers submit successfully, covered by a unit test on splitFormData
'Request a Showing' opens LeadFormModal (or CalendlyModal when a URL exists) pre-filled with the address and passes listing_id to submit-lead

DONE 2026-09-02.

PRE-APPROVAL. splitFormData now maps form answers through a ColumnMapping ({column, transform?, raw?}) rather than a bare string. preApproved goes through toPreapprovedBoolean — true for 'yes' and 'cash' (a cash buyer needs no approval), false otherwise — and the four-way answer is kept in form_data.preApprovalStatus, so the agent can still tell a cash offer from someone who needs a lender introduction. All four answers submit.

validateLeadData rejects a non-boolean `preapproved` and a non-uuid `listing_id`, with a new validateUuid helper. Both were 22P02s from the INSERT before, which submit-lead rethrew as a generic failure; they are now validation errors that name the field.

LISTING ATTACHMENT. LeadSubmissionData takes an optional listingId, sent as listing_id.
- ListingDetailModal: the two dead showing buttons are one button calling a new onRequestShowing(listing) prop — the Calendly branch was a raw target=_blank <a>, and 'Request a Showing' had no onClick at all.

Both send listingId and put the address in `data`, where splitFormData lifts it to property_address. ContactForm's description and message placeholder name the property, and its source becomes 'listing_inquiry'.
- ListingGallery's calendlyUrl prop, which it accepted and dropped, is deleted along with the call site that passed it.
- The Leads page card now shows property_address (LeadDetailModal already did), so a lead from a listing is identifiable in the list.

TESTS: src/lib/leadSubmission.test.ts (16) covers toPreapprovedBoolean, splitFormData over all four answers, the raw answer preserved in form_data, the other dedicated columns left untransformed, empty answers dropped, and submitLead's listing_id/property_address body. Verified to catch the regression: restoring the plain `preApproved: 'preapproved'` mapping turns 7 specs red. supabase/functions/_shared/validation.test.ts (13) covers validateUuid and the two new validateLeadData rules — it runs under vitest via the supabase/functions/**/*.test.ts include, since validation.ts touches no Deno globals at module scope.

VERIFICATION: npx tsc --noEmit 0 errors; npm run test:run 340 passed, 31 files (was 311); eslint 0 errors on the changed files (one pre-existing react/no-unescaped-entities warning in BuyerInquiryForm).

userStories.title: Anonymous visitors can insert leads directly into any agent's CRM, bypassing validation, encryption and the edge function
userStories.description: 20260806000005_squashed_baseline.sql:13525 creates policy "Anyone can submit leads" ON public.leads FOR INSERT WITH CHECK (true), and scripts/verify-schema.mjs:96 whitelists it in PUBLIC_BY_DESIGN as 'public lead-capture forms on every profile'. No public form uses it: leadSubmission.ts:92 and ContactBlock.tsx call submit-lead, which runs with the service role (index.ts:68). Verified live as anon: INSERT INTO leads (user_id, name, lead_type) VALUES (<any agent>, 'Spam Bot', 'buyer') succeeds with encrypted_email NULL, increments profiles.lead_count, writes a notifications row, a lead_activities row and three audit_logs rows, and fires trg_notify_lead_on_insert. Anyone holding the anon key, which ships in the bundle, can flood every agent's CRM at PostgREST speed with contact-less leads. Related: profiles.lead_count has an AFTER INSERT trigger and no DELETE counterpart (baseline:11208), so it only ever rises.
acceptanceCriteria: The "Anyone can submit leads" policy is dropped in a new migration and leads:INSERT is removed from PUBLIC_BY_DESIGN
An anon INSERT into leads is rejected, verified by executing it against the applied schema, and submit-lead still inserts successfully
npm run verify:schema passes with no new PUBLIC_BY_DESIGN entries
profiles.lead_count is either maintained by INSERT and DELETE triggers or replaced by a count(*) in the one place it is read
userStories.notes:
DONE 2026-09-02. Verified against a real Postgres 16 with the prelude and all migrations applied, not by inspection.

REPRODUCED FIRST. As `anon`, one statement:
  INSERT INTO public.leads (user_id, name, lead_type)
  VALUES ('<any agent id>', 'Spam Bot', 'buyer');   -- INSERT 0 1
produced a lead with encrypted_email NULL, profiles.lead_count 0 -> 1, one notifications row, one lead_activities row and three audit_logs rows. Nine triggers fire per insert. The agent id is on their public profile, so the target is not a secret either.

FIX: migration 20260902000001_leads_close_anon_insert.sql drops "Anyone can submit leads". It was FOR INSERT WITH CHECK (true) with no TO clause, which Postgres defaults to TO PUBLIC — and the anon key ships in the bundle. Nothing needed it: leadSubmission.ts and ContactBlock.tsx have both gone through the submit-lead edge function since US-069, and that runs with the service role, which is exempt from RLS.

VERIFIED AFTER THE FIX, all four executed against the applied schema:
  anon INSERT                      -> ERROR: new row violates RLS policy
  service_role INSERT (submit-lead)-> INSERT 0 1
  authenticated into another agent -> ERROR: new row violates RLS policy   (this was reachable through the same policy and is deliberately not restored)
  authenticated into their own CRM -> INSERT 0 1                            ("Users can insert their own leads")

PUBLIC_BY_DESIGN: leads:INSERT removed from scripts/verify-schema.mjs, replaced with a comment saying why it must not come back. verify:schema passes with no new entries, and the check is blocking rather than advisory — re-creating the policy makes it FAIL with "leads:INSERT ... is unconditional and reaches anon/authenticated", exit 1. Confirmed by creating it, running the script, and dropping it again.

LEAD_COUNT: on_lead_increment_profile_count was AFTER INSERT with no DELETE counterpart, so the counter only rose — including for spam the dropped policy allowed. Added decrement_profile_leads() and an AFTER DELETE trigger, both SECURITY DEFINER with search_path pinned to public, extensions, pg_temp. The migration also re-derives the column once so counts already inflated start correct. Verified: 3 leads -> lead_count 3; delete one -> 2; delete the rest -> 0. Worth recording that the column is read by nothing in src/ or supabase/functions/ today — it was kept and fixed rather than dropped because the dashboard may yet want it.

TYPES: src/integrations/supabase/types.ts regenerated; the only delta is the new decrement_profile_leads entry. gen-supabase-types --check and verify:schema both pass against the applied schema.

VERIFICATION: verify:schema 12/12 checks pass; validate-migrations OK (14 files); npx tsc --noEmit 0 errors; npm run test:run 340 passed.

NOT ADDRESSED HERE: rate limiting is still off, for the separate reason US-098 describes — the RPC is called with the wrong argument names and fails open. Dropping this policy removes the free path; US-098 is what puts a limiter in front of the paid one.

userStories.title: Rate limiting is silently disabled in every edge function: the RPC is called with the wrong argument names
userStories.description: supabase/functions/_shared/rate-limiter.ts:51-56 calls supabase.rpc('check_rate_limit', { p_ip_address, p_endpoint, p_max_requests, p_window_seconds }). The SQL function at baseline:638 is check_rate_limit(p_identifier text, p_limit_type text, p_max_requests integer, p_window_seconds integer). PostgREST cannot match the signature, returns 404, and the error branch at line 58 fails open with allowed: true. Every function that believes it is rate limited is not: submit-lead, check-username, create-checkout-session, create-portal-session, create-stripe-customer, report-stripe-usage, gdpr-export, generate-article, generate-listing-description, send-bio-analyzer-email, send-listing-generator-email, pii-crypto, verify-mfa. rate-limit/index.ts:139 uses the correct names, which is how it went unnoticed, and verify-schema.mjs:277-287 matches RPCs by name only, so the gate passes.
acceptanceCriteria: rate-limiter.ts passes p_identifier and p_limit_type, and a call against the applied schema returns an allowed/remaining/reset_at row
The submission and auth presets fail closed when the RPC errors; other presets log at error level with the PostgREST message rather than silently allowing
verify:schema compares each rpc() call's named arguments against pg_proc.proargnames and fails on a mismatch
An integration test (or the verify script) demonstrates the 11th call to submit-lead from one IP inside the window is rejected
cleanup_rate_limits() targets rate_limit_entries, the table check_rate_limit actually writes, or is replaced
userStories.notes:
DONE 2026-09-02. Verified against a real Postgres 16 with the prelude and all migrations applied.

REPRODUCED FIRST. The call rate-limiter.ts made, executed against the applied schema:
  SELECT * FROM check_rate_limit(p_ip_address => '1.2.3.4', p_endpoint => 'submit-lead', ...);
  ERROR: function public.check_rate_limit(p_ip_address => unknown, p_endpoint => unknown, ...) does not exist
The correct names return a row: t|4|<reset_at>. So the limiter errored on every call in all thirteen functions and the error branch returned allowed: true.

ORIGIN, worth recording because it explains the shape of the bug: p_ip_address and p_endpoint are the COLUMN names of public.rate_limits — an orphaned table from an earlier design that nothing has written to since. check_rate_limit reads and writes rate_limit_entries (identifier, limit_type). The limiter's own header comment said "rate_limits table", which is how the wrong names looked right.

FIXES:
1. rate-limiter.ts sends p_identifier / p_limit_type / p_max_requests / p_window_seconds.
2. RateLimitConfig gains failClosed. submission and auth set it true — for those an unavailable limiter means no control on abuse at all — general stays open so a read endpoint does not go down over a transient DB fault. Also set on generate-article's ad-hoc config, whose own comment says the limit exists to cap a model bill. gdpr-export's is deliberately left open: refusing a data-subject request is worse than allowing a second export in an hour. Every path now logs the PostgREST message at error level with "failing open"/"failing closed"; the old code logged error?.message and returned allowed: true for everything, which is how a call that never once succeeded went unnoticed.
3. Migration 20260902000002 repoints cleanup_rate_limits() at rate_limit_entries (deleting on window_end, the column check_rate_limit maintains) with search_path pinned. It had been deleting from rate_limits, so it ran successfully, removed nothing, and rate_limit_entries grew without bound. The orphan table is left in place — dropping it belongs with US-124 — but nothing references it now.

VERIFY:SCHEMA — two new checks, both demonstrated to fail on the original defect:
- "every rpc() call's named arguments exist on the function" reads pg_proc.proargnames, filtered by proargmodes to input parameters only (proargnames includes OUT columns, so an unfiltered list would have accepted a call passing `allowed` as an argument). Restoring p_ip_address/p_endpoint makes it FAIL and exit 1, naming the file and listing what the function accepts. The scanner is depth- and ternary-aware: nested objects (p_details: { count: n }) and conditionals (p_action: cond ? 'a' : 'b') were both producing false positives across every log_audit_event call in the tree. Non-literal argument objects, spreads and computed keys are reported as notes rather than guessed at.
- "check_rate_limit refuses the 11th call in a window" runs ten calls at a limit of ten, asserts each is allowed with remaining counting 9..0, asserts the eleventh returns false,0, then expires the row and asserts cleanup_rate_limits() collects it. Reverting the cleanup fix makes it FAIL with "cleanup_rate_limits() left an expired rate_limit_entries row behind".

TESTS: supabase/functions/_shared/rate-limiter.test.ts (9) asserts the exact argument object sent to rpc(), the 'unknown' identifier substitution, a refusal passed through, and the failure matrix — submission and auth refuse, general allows, an exception and an empty result set are both treated as failures rather than allowances, and the PostgREST message is logged.

VERIFICATION: verify:schema 14/14; validate-migrations OK (15 files); npx tsc --noEmit 0 errors; npm run test:run 349 passed, 32 files (was 340); gen-supabase-types --check up to date. `deno check` over the edge functions is not runnable here (no Deno in this environment) and remains CI's job; the change to rate-limiter.ts is plain TypeScript with one added optional field.

NOT DONE: criterion 4 asks for the 11th call to SUBMIT-LEAD to be rejected, i.e. through the deployed function over HTTP. What is demonstrated is the SQL function refusing the 11th call, plus a unit test that the limiter sends the right arguments and honours a refusal. The HTTP hop between them needs a deployed function — same environmental blocker as US-090.

userStories.title: Lead notifications: no contact details in the email, two emails per lead, preferences ignored, and a trigger that has never fired
userStories.description: Four defects in one path. (1) notify-lead/index.ts:76 re-reads the lead with select('*') and lines 119-120 pass lead.email and lead.phone, both dropped by 20260901000001, so the text body reads 'Email: undefined' and the HTML row filter drops both contact rows; the agent gets a New Lead email with no way to reply. (2) submit-lead/index.ts:263-321 emails the agent directly AND trg_notify_lead_on_insert calls notify-lead for the same row, so when both work every lead sends two emails. (3) submit-lead ignores notification_preferences.leads while notify-lead honours 'off' and 'daily_digest' (index.ts:101-104), and no digest job exists, so agents on daily_digest are never emailed at all. (4) The trigger (baseline:2405-2410) returns early unless the GUCs app.settings.functions_url and app.settings.service_role_key are set; no live migration sets them (the instruction is in archive/20260525000001), so in practice it has never fired, and if it were set as documented the service-role key would live as a plaintext database GUC. Also _shared/email.ts:26-30,54-59 swallows every failure including a missing RESEND_API_KEY, and notify-lead:131-140 logs 'success' before knowing whether anything sent.
acceptanceCriteria: Exactly one notification path exists: submit-lead (and useLeads.createLead for manually added leads) calls notify-lead explicitly and trg_notify_lead_on_insert plus notify_new_lead's GUC dependency are dropped
notify-lead decrypts encrypted_email and encrypted_phone with the _shared/encryption.ts counterpart before rendering; the email shows the lead's email and phone
notification_preferences.leads = 'off' sends nothing; 'daily_digest' is treated as 'instant' until a digest job exists, and that is stated in the settings UI
sendEmail returns { ok, providerId, error }; a send failure or missing RESEND_API_KEY in production is logged at error level and recorded, not reported as success
Each agent email sent for a lead is recorded as a lead_activities row of activity_type 'email' so the timeline shows it
npm run test:run and deno check both pass
userStories.notes:
MOSTLY DONE 2026-09-02. Five of six criteria met; one deliberately deviated from, with reasoning below. Schema work verified against a real Postgres 16 with every migration applied.

(1) NO CONTACT DETAILS. notify-lead passed lead.email and lead.phone — columns 20260901000001 dropped — so the agent's New Lead email read "Email: undefined" and the HTML contact rows were filtered out. It now decrypts encrypted_email / encrypted_phone through _shared/encryption.ts decryptSecret() before rendering.

(2) TWO EMAILS PER LEAD. submit-lead composed and sent its own agent email while trg_notify_lead_on_insert called notify-lead for the same row. That block is deleted; submit-lead now POSTs { lead_id } to notify-lead with the service-role key from its own environment. Worth noting what went with it: the inline HTML interpolated the visitor's name and message unescaped, which the shared createLeadNotificationEmail template does not.

(3) PREFERENCES. notify-lead skipped anything that was not 'instant', so every agent on 'daily_digest' was never emailed about a lead at all — there is no digest job. 'off' now suppresses; 'daily_digest' sends instantly, which is the failure mode that loses no leads. Said plainly in the settings UI: the option reads "Not available yet — currently sends instantly, like Instant" rather than "One summary email per day". Two stale `as never` / `as {...}` casts in that component are gone too — notification_preferences has been in types.ts throughout (types.ts:3414), same pattern as US-094.

(4) THE TRIGGER THAT NEVER FIRED. Confirmed against the applied schema: after every migration, current_setting('app.settings.functions_url', true) is NULL, so notify_lead_on_insert() returned early every time. Migration 20260902000003 drops the trigger and the function. It is not repaired because the documented setup stores the service-role key as a plaintext GUC readable through any SECURITY DEFINER function — worse than the notification being broken. trg_notify_new_lead / notify_new_lead() are a different trigger, take no GUCs, insert the in-app notifications row, and are untouched.

(5) SENDEMAIL. Returns { ok, providerId, error } instead of void. A missing RESEND_API_KEY is an error in production (a warning elsewhere, so local dev needs no key), a non-2xx from Resend reports the status and body, a network error reports its message — none of them throw, so a notification failure still cannot roll back the lead. notify-lead logs audit status 'success'/'failure' from the actual result rather than unconditionally.

(6) TIMELINE. Every agent notification writes a lead_activities row of activity_type 'email' with the subject and recipient, titled for success or failure. Verified against the schema that the insert is accepted and sits alongside the existing 'form_submission' activity. A failed send now also returns 502 rather than 200.

DEVIATION — useLeads does NOT call notify-lead, and the criterion asked it to. Two reasons, both stated rather than worked around: notify-lead notifies leads.user_id, so on this path it would email an agent about a lead they had just typed into their own CRM; and reaching it from the browser means accepting a user session on a function US-078 deliberately restricted to the service role. The code carries this reasoning at the call site, with the note that team assignment, if it ever needs to notify, should do so from the assignment trigger addressed to leads.assigned_to.

TESTS: supabase/functions/_shared/email.test.ts (8) covers the missing-key path in and out of production, the provider id on success, a 422 reported rather than swallowed, a network error, and escapeHtml. It runs under vitest with a stubbed Deno global — the module reads Deno.env inside the function, not at module scope.

VERIFICATION: npx tsc --noEmit 0 errors; npm run test:run 357 passed, 33 files (was 349); verify:schema 14/14; validate-migrations OK (16 files); gen-supabase-types --check up to date. `deno check` is CI's — no Deno in this environment — so the edge-function changes are unverified by a type-checker here; they are plain TypeScript with no new imports beyond decryptSecret, which notify-lead's sibling functions already use.

userStories.title: Three lead-activity RPCs and one workflow node write columns that do not exist
userStories.description: log_lead_activity, log_lead_call and log_lead_email (baseline ~2177, ~2236, ~2291) all end with UPDATE public.leads SET last_contacted_at = NOW(). leads has contacted_at, never last_contacted_at; plpgsql resolves the name at run time, so the first real call raises 'column last_contacted_at does not exist' after the activity row is inserted and the whole transaction rolls back. It is latent only because nothing in src/ calls them yet (see US-102, which will). supabase/functions/execute-workflow/index.ts:69-87 does `if (score) updates.score = score` and updates leads; there is no score column (lead_scores is the table), so any workflow that sets a score fails. notify-lead/index.ts:35-36,124 reads lead.score ?? lead.lead_score, both absent, so the score badge never renders. verify:schema checks columns referenced by triggers, but not by plain functions or by edge-function payloads.

DONE 2026-09-02. Verified against a real Postgres 16 with every migration applied.

REPRODUCED FIRST:
  SELECT log_lead_call('<lead>', 'connected', 120, 'Talked through budget');
  ERROR: column "last_contacted_at" of relation "leads" does not exist
  CONTEXT: PL/pgSQL function log_lead_call(uuid,text,integer,text) line 40
The activity row is inserted before that UPDATE, so the exception rolled back both — the agent would log a call and lose the call and the timestamp together.

CORRECTION TO THE STORY'S PREMISE. It says "nothing in src/ calls them yet". src/hooks/useLeadActivities.ts calls all three (lines 139, 163, 188, 213). What is true is that no component imports that hook, so there is no reachable caller — the defect is latent because the UI is not wired up, not because the call sites do not exist. US-102 mounts it, which is still the reason this had to land first.

MIGRATION 20260902000004 rewrites all three to set contacted_at, using COALESCE(contacted_at, NOW()) rather than NOW(). The column records FIRST contact — Leads.tsx measures response time from it and the SLA card keys off it — so overwriting it on every follow-up would make an agent look faster the more often they called. Verified: all three now return an activity id, the timeline shows call/email/meeting/note alongside the trigger's form_submission, contacted_at is set, and a second call leaves it unchanged.

EXECUTE-WORKFLOW. The update_lead node did `if (score) updates.score = score` against `leads`, which has no score column, so a workflow setting a score also failed to apply the status and notes beside it. It now upserts lead_scores (lead_id, user_id, score, priority, variant, scored_at) on the lead_id unique constraint, reading user_id from the lead rather than trusting workflow context, clamping the score to the 0-100 CHECK, deriving priority within the hot/warm/cold CHECK, and recording variant 'rules' — a workflow-set score is a rule, not a model prediction.

NOTIFY-LEAD read lead.score ?? lead.lead_score, neither of which exists, so the score badge never rendered. It now reads lead_scores.score with maybeSingle(); a missing row is normal (scoring may not have run) and renders no badge.

VERIFY:SCHEMA — two new checks, 15 -> 16 total, both demonstrated against the original defect:
- "plpgsql function bodies reference only real columns" parses UPDATE ... SET and INSERT INTO ... (cols) targets out of every plpgsql body in public, not just trigger functions, which is the gap that let this through. Restoring the broken UPDATE makes it FAIL with "log_lead_call: UPDATE leads SET last_contacted_at — no such column", exit 1. Conservative by design: only tables the catalog knows and simple column lists are checked, and a body that defeats the parse is skipped rather than guessed at.
- "log_lead_activity / _call / _email run against a real lead" executes all three as the owning user against a fixture lead, asserts the three activity types land, asserts contacted_at is set, and asserts a later call does not move it. A body parse cannot see an ownership guard that never passes or a CHECK constraint; this can. Confirmed it fails with the original ERROR when the broken function is restored.

VERIFICATION: verify:schema 16/16; validate-migrations OK (17 files); npx tsc --noEmit 0 errors; npm run test:run 357 passed; gen-supabase-types --check up to date. `deno check` remains CI's — no Deno in this environment — so the two edge-function changes are unverified by a type-checker here.

userStories.title: Lead detail modal shows the previous lead's status and draft note, and status changes never record when the agent made contact
userStories.description: LeadDetailModal.tsx:109-110 initialises status and note with useState(lead?.status) once; Leads.tsx:790-797 keeps a single instance mounted and swaps the lead prop, so opening a 'converted' lead then a 'new' one shows Converted on the second, with the previous half-typed note still in the box. Only loadNotes() re-runs. Status changes (LeadDetailModal.tsx:149-154, Leads.tsx:214-218) do .update({ status }) and nothing else: no code in src/ writes contacted_at or closed_at. first_responded_at is set by the set_lead_first_responded_at trigger only on new -> anything, so an agent who taps the tel:/mailto:/sms: links (349-376) and calls the lead straight away still shows 'No response . 3h' and drags the Avg Response KPI down. Bulk-setting leads back to 'new' (Leads.tsx:559) silently keeps first_responded_at.
acceptanceCriteria: The modal re-initialises status and note when lead.id changes (key={lead.id} or an effect)
Tapping call, email or text from the card or modal logs a lead_activities row via log_lead_call/log_lead_email and moves a 'new' lead to 'contacted' with contacted_at set
Setting status to converted or lost writes closed_at; resetting to new clears first_responded_at and contacted_at
Response time on the Leads page and Overview reflects the first contact action, not only a dropdown change
A component test opens two leads in sequence and asserts the second shows its own status
userStories.notes:
DONE 2026-09-02. Component behaviour covered by tests; the SQL side verified against a real Postgres.

(1) STALE MODAL STATE. LeadDetailModal initialised `status` and `note` with useState, which reads its initial value only on mount, while Leads.tsx keeps one instance mounted and swaps the lead prop. An effect keyed on lead.id now re-initialises status, note, notes and selectedResponse. Keyed on the id rather than the object, so a refetch returning an equal-but-new row does not wipe what the agent is typing. Worth stating plainly: the consequence was not only a wrong badge — saving from that state wrote one lead's note onto another.

(2) CONTACT ACTIONS, both surfaces. The mailto:/tel:/sms: links had no side effect, so an agent who phoned a lead a minute after it arrived still read "No response · 3h". src/hooks/useLeadContactAction.ts holds the behaviour and is used by the detail modal AND the Leads page card, so the two cannot drift: a 'new' lead moves to 'contacted' with contacted_at set, and the timeline row goes through log_lead_call / log_lead_email / log_lead_activity. The link is never intercepted — the href fires and the dialer opens — and a failure to record is logged without blocking the call. On the card the click also stopPropagation()s, which it did not before: tapping a phone number used to open the detail modal behind the dialer.

CallOutcome gained 'initiated'. The existing four (answered/voicemail/no_answer/busy) are outcomes an agent reports afterwards; tapping tel: establishes only that the dialer opened, and recording 'answered' would put a fact in the timeline nobody established. There is no CHECK constraint on lead_activities.call_outcome.

(3) TRANSITION RULES, in one place. src/lib/leadStatus.ts holds buildLeadStatusPatch and buildContactPatch, used by the modal and the bulk action alike. converted/lost/closed write closed_at; moving back into the pipeline clears it; the first move into contact sets contacted_at and a later one leaves it (it records FIRST contact, per US-100); a reset to 'new' clears first_responded_at, contacted_at and closed_at. When no lead row is supplied — the bulk action holds none — the rules depending on the previous value are skipped rather than guessed at, while the clearing rules still apply.

(4) RESPONSE TIME. Verified against the applied schema, the whole cycle: a 'new' lead updated with the contact patch gets first_responded_at from set_lead_first_responded_at; converting sets closed_at; the reset-to-'new' patch clears all three (the trigger does not fire, since NEW.status = 'new'); and a subsequent move to 'contacted' sets first_responded_at again. That last step never worked — a reopened lead kept a first_responded_at the trigger could never re-set, so it counted as responded to forever and could never contribute to the KPI again.

TESTS: leadStatus.test.ts (12) covers every rule including the bulk case. LeadDetailModal.test.tsx (4) mounts the modal once and swaps the prop exactly as the page does — the second lead shows its own status, the half-typed note does not carry across, tapping the phone number writes status 'contacted' with contacted_at, and it logs log_lead_call with outcome 'initiated'. Leads.test.tsx gained two: the card records the response, and the contact link no longer opens the modal behind it. Verified to catch the regression: removing the re-init effect turns two of the modal specs red.

VERIFICATION: npx tsc --noEmit 0 errors; npm run test:run 375 passed, 35 files (was 357); verify:schema 16/16; eslint 0 errors on the changed files (one pre-existing exhaustive-deps warning on the older loadNotes effect).

userStories.title: The activity timeline is dead: the modal reads lead_notes while every trigger writes lead_activities
userStories.description: src/hooks/useLeadActivities.ts is 336 lines with seven mutations and zero importers. LeadDetailModal.tsx:129-133 loads lead_notes and, on status change (line 163), writes a system note there, while the DB trigger on_lead_status_change (baseline:11215) writes a lead_activities row for the same event. auto_log_lead_creation (baseline:11201) writes 'Lead created' to lead_activities too. Two stores, one displayed, so the timeline the agent sees is missing every trigger-logged event and every call/email logged by US-101. useLeadsActivitySummaries, which would show 'last contacted' on the list, is likewise unused.
