userStories.title: Unbreak sign-in: the missing onboarding column and the auth-lock deadlock
userStories.description: Both /auth/login and /auth/register dead-ended at /onboarding/wizard for anyone with a session, and the app hung for logged-in users. Two independent causes, confirmed against production on 2026-09-03. (1) public.profiles has no onboarding_completed_at column in production: ?select=onboarding_completed_at returns 42703 and the table is exactly one column short of the squashed baseline, because archive/20260525000006_onboarding_completed.sql was never applied there and CI only ever builds a database from supabase/migrations/*.sql, where the baseline supplies it. So select('*') returned a row with no such key, RequireAuth's `!profile.onboarding_completed_at` was true for EVERY user, and the wizard could not clear it either: buildOnboardingProfileUpdate always names the column, PostgREST rejects an update naming an unknown column, and the whole statement failed with 'Failed to save your information'. (2) useAuthStore.initialize passed an async callback to supabase.auth.onAuthStateChange that awaited supabase.from('profiles'). supabase-js runs those callbacks holding the origin-wide lock:sb-api-auth-token Web Lock, and any supabase call needs an access token, which takes the same lock. navigator.locks.query() on agentbio.net showed one held lock and a permanently pending waiter, the holder living in another tab: RequireAuth sat on 'Verifying session...' forever and Login's button sat on 'Signing in...' forever, in every tab, until the poisoned one was closed.
acceptanceCriteria: profiles.onboarding_completed_at exists in production and is backfilled: `select id from profiles where onboarding_completed_at is null` returns only accounts that genuinely have not finished the wizard, and no established agent is routed to /onboarding/wizard on login
Completing or skipping the wizard writes onboarding_completed_at and lands on /dashboard without bouncing back

No onAuthStateChange callback anywhere calls supabase; a lint or test fails if one does. After a hard reload as a signed-in user, navigator.locks.query() shows no lock:sb-api-auth-token held once the page has settled
RequireAuth treats an ABSENT onboarding_completed_at key as unknown rather than as 'not onboarded', so a partial or rehydrated profile cannot trap a user (covered by a test)
The login form is interactive on arrival: its button reads 'Sign In', not 'Signing in...', before a submit
userStories.notes: Code fix landed 2026-09-03: 20260903000001_profiles_onboarding_completed_at.sql (idempotent, so a no-op on a database built from the baseline), the setTimeout(..., 0) escape in useAuthStore.initialize, the key-presence guard in RequireAuth, Register.tsx handing off to /dashboard instead of naming the wizard, and a local isSubmitting in Login.tsx. STILL OPEN: the migration has to be applied to production by hand. Migrations are not deployed by CI - verify-backend only applies them to a throwaway Postgres - which is how the drift survived this long, and that gap deserves its own story. Anyone whose tab is currently holding the auth lock must close every agentbio.net tab once, since the deadlocked client outlives the deploy.

userStories.title: Listing photos: a stringified jsonb column, a placeholder that is not a file, a bucket that is not a bucket
userStories.description: The Listings dashboard and every public profile drew no photos. Three faults on one path, all confirmed against production on 2026-09-03. (1) sample-data-service wrote `photos: JSON.stringify([...])` into a jsonb column, so the column held the JSON *string* '"[\"https://...\"]"' and not an array. toStringList tests Array.isArray, a string fails it, and every seeded listing came back with zero photos; all four listings on the owner account had photos nobody could see. (2) getImageUrl's fallback was '/placeholder-property.jpg' and no such file has ever existed in public/. Cloudflare Pages answered it with the SPA's index.html under a JPEG content type, 5.8 KB of markup where an image should be, so the fallback drew a broken-image icon - including from the onError handlers whose only job was to replace a broken image. Nine call sites referenced it. (3) Every getImageUrl/getImageUrls call passed bucket 'listings', which is not a bucket in any environment; 20260808000005 standardised on 'listing-photos'. Latent only because uploads store an absolute URL that getImageUrl returns untouched.
acceptanceCriteria: listings.photos is a jsonb array in every row: `select count(*) from listings where jsonb_typeof(photos) = 'string'` returns 0 in production, and the dashboard and public profile render the seeded photos
A write that stringifies the array is rejected by the listings_photos_is_array check rather than silently emptying the gallery at the reader
toStringList parses a JSON-encoded array as well as a real one, covered by a test that uses the exact shape production stored
The placeholder resolves to a real image: /placeholder-property.svg is in dist/ after a build and returns image/svg+xml, and no source file references placeholder-property.jpg
No caller names a storage bucket that does not exist; listing photo URLs are built against listing-photos
userStories.notes: Fixed 2026-09-03: real arrays in sample-data-service, 20260903000002_repair_double_encoded_listing_photos.sql (per-row repair with exception handling plus a NOT VALID check constraint), the JSON-string branch in toStringList, public/placeholder-property.svg with PLACEHOLDER_PROPERTY_IMAGE and LISTING_PHOTO_BUCKET exported from lib/images, and both applied at all nine call sites. The repair was exercised against a real postgres:16 with all 32 migrations applied: one double-encoded row repaired, a correct array untouched, an unparseable string left alone without aborting, and a stringified insert afterwards rejected by the constraint. STILL OPEN: apply the migration to production. See US-146 for why it is not there already.

userStories.title: Production is not the schema in this repo: 11 missing tables, no storage buckets, undeployed functions
userStories.description: Reconciling production against supabase/migrations on 2026-09-03 found the drift is systemic, not the single column US-144 patched. PostgREST's own OpenAPI spec at api.agentbio.net/rest/v1/ lists 136 definitions, of which 12 are views; against the 136 tables the migrations create, production is missing account_deletion_log, invoices, lead_routing_rules, mortgage_calculations, notifications, query_metrics, rate_limits, stripe_processed_events, team_members, team_round_robin and teams. (lead_notes is also absent and should be: 20260902000005 folds it into lead_activities.) The dashboard 404s on notifications on every load, twice. Storage is worse: GET /storage/v1/bucket/listing-photos and /avatars both return 'Bucket not found', so NO bucket exists and every photo and avatar upload fails - 20260808000005 was never applied. Edge functions are behind too: functions.agentbio.net/get-sessions and /gdpr-deletion return 404 and /pii-crypto returns 500, though all three exist in supabase/functions. Ten of the eleven missing tables come from the squashed baseline (US-060), which is the tell: the baseline was written from the migration history rather than dumped from production, so everything the archived migrations added and never applied is missing there and present in CI. verify-backend applies migrations to a throwaway Postgres and asserts against that, so it is green on a database nobody uses.
acceptanceCriteria: A documented reconciliation: for each of the 11 tables, the storage buckets and each undeployed function, either it is applied to production or there is a recorded decision that it is not wanted
Photo and avatar upload work end to end in production: a real upload lands in listing-photos and the returned public URL 200s
The dashboard makes no 404 request on load; notifications either exists or the client stops querying it
pii-crypto returns 200 for its own caller, or decryptOwnProfilePhone stops calling it
CI can tell that production has drifted: a job compares the applied production schema against the migrations and fails on a difference, rather than only verifying a database built from scratch
Migrations reach production by a defined route (a deploy step or a written runbook), not by hand with no record of what was applied
userStories.notes: Evidence gathered read-only from the browser against production: the PostgREST OpenAPI spec for the table list, /storage/v1/bucket/<name> for the buckets, and the console log from the user's own dashboard session for the function 404s and the pii-crypto 500. US-144 and US-145 each patched one symptom of this; both are blocked on the same manual apply. Do this before either of them is called done.

userStories.title: Nothing public is prerendered: Googlebot gets an empty shell and one identical title for all 44 URLs
userStories.description: The single root cause behind 33 clicks in 16 months. agentbio.net is a pure client-rendered Vite SPA with no SSG, SSR or prerender step anywhere - package.json and vite.config.ts contain no prerender/ssg/react-snap/puppeteer dependency, and public/_redirects is `/* /index.html 200`, so every one of the 44 sitemap URLs returns the identical shell. index.html:80 hardcodes ONE <title> ('Real Estate Agent Bio Page Builder | Turn Instagram Followers into Leads - AgentBio') for the whole site; the real per-page titles, descriptions, canonicals and JSON-LD are produced by react-helmet-async (SEOHead.tsx, seo/PageSEO.tsx, blog/ArticleSEO.tsx) and therefore only exist after hydration. Googlebot's first pass sees an empty div and a title shared with 43 other URLs, then has to queue the page for the render service. The GSC export of 2026-09-08 shows the consequence exactly: all 23 /for/{city} pages, all 5 /features/* pages and all 3 /vs/* pages - 31 pages, every one of them in the sitemap - have ZERO impressions across the full 16 months. Pages.csv lists every page with at least one impression (it reaches down to /accessibility with 1), and not one of the 31 appears. The second signature is high rank with no clicks, which is what a duplicated SERP title produces: /pricing sits at position 4.77 on 122 impressions with 1 click (0.82% CTR, where position 5 should return 6-9%), /blog/link-hub-for-leasing-agents at position 3.00 with 0 clicks, /blog/home-selling-link-hub at position 5.23 with 0 clicks. Fix the delivery, not the meta components - those are already correct and already carry canonical, og and schema.
acceptanceCriteria: A postbuild prerender step renders every static public route to its own HTML file under dist/ (e.g. dist/pricing/index.html, dist/vs/linktree/index.html, dist/for/miami-real-estate-agents/index.html). Use the playwright already in devDependencies (^1.57.0) against a local `vite preview`; do NOT add puppeteer or a second browser dependency

The route list is derived from a single exported source of truth, not hand-maintained twice: static routes from a routes manifest and the 23 /for/{slug} pages from the existing LOCATIONS array in src/data/locations.ts (26 entries)

Each prerendered file contains the page's own post-hydration <title>, <meta name="description">, <link rel="canonical"> and JSON-LD in the served HTML, not the index.html defaults. Verify by asserting the title in dist/pricing/index.html differs from the title in dist/index.html
The prerendered HTML still hydrates without a React mismatch warning: loading a prerendered route in a browser logs no 'did not match' / hydration error in the console

Cloudflare Pages serves the static file rather than the SPA fallback for a prerendered route - confirm the `/* /index.html 200` rule in public/_redirects does not shadow the emitted files (static assets are matched before redirects; add a test or a documented check)
Routes behind auth (/dashboard/*, /admin/*, /onboarding/*) and the dynamic tenant routes (/:username, /p/:slug, /:username/review) are NOT prerendered
`npm run build` still succeeds and the prerender step fails the build loudly if a route renders an error page or an empty root
Typecheck passes: tsc --noEmit succeeds
userStories.notes: This is the unlock - US-148 through US-158 are largely wasted effort until it ships, so it goes first and nothing else in this batch should be started before it passes. Do not rewrite SEOHead/PageSEO/ArticleSEO; they already emit the right tags and the only defect is that a crawler never runs them. Watch build time: 44 routes through a headless browser is the slow part of CI - render them concurrently with a bounded pool. Keep the prerender script in scripts/ alongside the existing check-bundle-size.mjs / verify-schema.mjs and match their .mjs + node style.

userStories.title: Blog articles are fetched from Supabase in the browser, so the body of every post is invisible on first crawl
userStories.description: src/pages/BlogArticle.tsx:26 queries `.from('articles')` at runtime, so a blog URL returns the same empty shell as everything else and the article text only exists after the bundle executes AND a Supabase round-trip resolves - the worst case for indexing. The GSC export shows what this costs: the 25 blog posts other than the single 2024 post earned 2 clicks combined across 16 months. The exception proves the mechanism is survivable but expensive - /blog/how-real-estate-agents-use-link-in-bio-to-generate-more-leads-in-2024 pulled 162 impressions and 6 clicks at position 11.09, which is 18% of the entire site's clicks from one post that has had long enough for the render queue to reach it. Extend the US-147 prerender to article routes by fetching published articles from Supabase at BUILD time and emitting real HTML per slug.
acceptanceCriteria: The prerender step fetches published rows from the `articles` table at build time (id, title, slug, excerpt, content, featured_image_url, author_id, published_at, updated_at, seo_title, seo_description, tags) and emits dist/blog/<slug>/index.html for each
The article body text is present in the emitted HTML - grep for a distinctive sentence from an article's content in its prerendered file and find it

Each article file carries its own <title> (seo_title falling back to title), meta description (seo_description falling back to excerpt), canonical, og:type=article, og:image and Article JSON-LD, matching what blog/ArticleSEO.tsx produces client-side
dist/blog/index.html (the listing) and the /blog/category/:category routes are prerendered from the same fetched set

The build degrades safely when Supabase is unreachable or credentials are absent: it must NOT silently emit zero article pages - either fail the build or reuse a committed snapshot, and say which in the log
Publishing an article triggers a rebuild: a documented Cloudflare Pages deploy hook fired from the existing article publish path, so a new post reaches the index without a manual deploy
Typecheck passes: tsc --noEmit succeeds
userStories.notes: Depends on US-147. Use the anon key and rely on RLS - do not put a service-role key into the build. `articles` is the table; `blog_posts` has never existed (see CLAUDE.md). The 'fail loudly on zero articles' criterion is the important one: a build that quietly ships an empty blog is exactly how the current sitemap ended up with no articles in it. VERIFIED AGAINST A STUB PostgREST, not production - no database credentials on the build machine. Two human steps remain, both needing credentials: run 'npm run articles:snapshot' somewhere the database is reachable and commit scripts/data/articles.snapshot.json, and create the Cloudflare Pages deploy hook and set CLOUDFLARE_DEPLOY_HOOK_URL in the Supabase edge function secrets (docs/deploy/BLOG_PRERENDERING.md). Until the snapshot is committed, CI's build and bundle-size jobs carry PRERENDER_ALLOW_NO_ARTICLES=1, which omits the blog rather than emitting empty posts; a deploy must never set it.

userStories.title: The sitemap lists 44 URLs, none of which is a blog post, and one of which is a soft 404
userStories.description: public/sitemap.xml is a static hand-edited file - 44 <loc> entries, every lastmod reading 2026-02-08, file last modified 2026-07-14 - and robots.txt points Google at it. Three defects. (1) Not one of the 25+ blog articles is listed; only /blog itself. (2) https://agentbio.net/features is listed but there is no `/features` route in App.tsx - only the five /features/* children at App.tsx:202-206 - so it falls through to `path="*"` and returns the NotFound page under a 200, a soft 404 submitted to Google on purpose. /llms.txt is listed as a page and is not one. (3) Five real routes are missing: /cookies, /privacy-choices, /accessibility, /blog/category/:category and the article URLs. Meanwhile two Supabase edge functions that generate sitemaps - supabase/functions/generate-sitemap/index.ts (309 lines) and supabase/functions/sitemap/index.ts (187 lines) - both exist, duplicate each other, and neither is what agentbio.net/sitemap.xml serves. They are dead code.
acceptanceCriteria: sitemap.xml is generated during the build from the same route source of truth as US-147 plus the articles fetched in US-148, with a real per-URL lastmod (articles use articles.updated_at)
Every URL in the generated sitemap resolves to a prerendered file that is not the NotFound page - assert this in the build, so a /features-style soft 404 can never be submitted again
/llms.txt is removed from the sitemap (it stays served, it is not a page); /features is removed or given a real route
All published article URLs appear in the sitemap

The two dead edge functions are resolved: either delete supabase/functions/generate-sitemap and supabase/functions/sitemap, or wire exactly one of them to the served path and delete the other. Two generators and a third static file is the state that produced this bug
robots.txt still points at the one sitemap that is actually served
Typecheck passes: tsc --noEmit succeeds
userStories.notes: Depends on US-147 and US-148. US-124 (dead code sweep) should be told which of the two sitemap functions survives. Resubmitting in GSC is a human step - note it in progress.txt rather than claiming it. Reality differed from the description: there were FIVE sitemap implementations, not two - public/sitemap.xml (the only one served), the two edge functions, an unrouted src/pages/Sitemap.tsx, and a dead generateSitemap() export in src/lib/seo.ts. All four dead ones deleted. /features needed a 301 in public/_redirects as well as removal from the sitemap, because the URL still answered 200 with the SPA 404 page.

userStories.title: CI gate: fail the build when a prerendered page has a missing or duplicated title, description or canonical
userStories.description: The reason 44 URLs shipped with one shared title for a year is that nothing checked. US-147 fixes today's HTML; this keeps it fixed. Add an automated assertion over the built dist/ that every prerendered page carries a unique, non-empty title and description and a self-referencing canonical, and run it in CI so the regression cannot return silently.
acceptanceCriteria: A test (vitest or a scripts/*.mjs invoked by CI) walks every *.html under dist/ and asserts: <title> present, non-empty, and not equal to the index.html title unless the file IS index.html
Asserts <meta name="description"> present, non-empty, and unique across pages (a small allowlist is acceptable for genuine near-duplicates, but it must be explicit and named)
Asserts <link rel="canonical"> present and pointing at the page's own absolute URL, not at the homepage
Asserts the file is not the NotFound page and its <body> is not empty
The check runs in the existing GitHub Actions workflow and fails the build on violation
Running it against the current pre-US-147 output would fail - demonstrate that with a test fixture, so the gate is known to have teeth
An `npm run verify:seo` script exists, matching the style of the existing verify:schema / size-check scripts
Typecheck passes: tsc --noEmit succeeds
userStories.notes: Depends on US-147. Keep it in the same spirit as the existing verify:schema / size-check scripts: a plain node script with a clear failure message naming the offending file. Teeth demonstrated twice: seo-audit.test.ts rejects a reproduction of the pre-US-147 output on all four counts, and a real dist/pricing/index.html corrupted to carry the homepage title with no canonical was caught and exited 1. vitest.config.ts now includes scripts/**/*.test.ts.

userStories.title: Auth and legal pages absorb 22% of impressions, and robots.txt is blocking the fix
userStories.description: 321 of 1,481 impressions (21.7%) went to pages with no commercial value: /auth/login 114, /dmca 72, /terms 56, /privacy 40, /acceptable-use 39. /dmca ranks for 'dmca copyright office ia' at position 70.88 and /auth/register has 42 impressions. The subtle part is that robots.txt already says `Disallow: /auth/` and the login page is indexed anyway - Disallow prevents crawling, not indexing, so Google indexes the URL from links alone and can never see a noindex directive because it is forbidden from fetching the page that would carry one. Blocking harder makes this worse, not better. Now that US-147 puts real meta in the served HTML, the correct fix is available: let Googlebot fetch these routes and tell it not to index them.
acceptanceCriteria: Remove `Disallow: /auth/` from public/robots.txt so Googlebot can fetch the auth routes and read their directives (keep /api/ and /dashboard/ disallowed)
Every /auth/* route emits <meta name="robots" content="noindex, follow"> in its prerendered HTML - the SEOHead component already supports a noindex prop, so wire it rather than adding a mechanism
The auth routes are prerendered (so the directive is visible without JS) but excluded from sitemap.xml
Legal pages (/privacy, /terms, /dmca, /acceptable-use, /cookies, /privacy-choices, /accessibility) stay indexable but are given a low sitemap priority and are excluded from internal-link prominence
US-150's uniqueness gate accounts for the noindexed pages rather than failing on them
Typecheck passes: tsc --noEmit succeeds
userStories.notes: Depends on US-147 and US-149. Do not add `noindex` to the legal pages - they are legitimate pages and removing them from the index does not redistribute their impressions to anything. The 22% figure is a symptom of a thin site, and the cure is US-155/156 having something better to rank; this story only stops the auth URLs from competing. Applied at the route via src/components/auth/AuthRouteSEO.tsx rather than editing seven components. /auth/callback is deliberately NOT prerendered: it redirects, so its snapshot was the login page, which verify:seo caught as a shared title. X-Robots-Tag on /auth/* in public/_headers covers it. Footer bottom-bar legal nav removed (was a third sitewide link set to the same pages).

userStories.title: The homepage title targets the one query the product cannot satisfy
userStories.description: index.html:80 and the homepage SEOHead both read 'Real Estate Agent Bio Page Builder | Turn Instagram Followers into Leads - AgentBio', and the GSC query report shows exactly who that attracts. The largest impression cluster is informational and wrong-intent: 'real estate agent bio' 82 impressions at position 88.56, 'agent bio' 60 at 7.33, 'luxury real estate agent bio' 6 at 63.33, 'real estate bio new agent' 4 at 105.25, 'real estate agent bio for new agents' 3 at 37, 'professional real estate agent bio examples' 2 at 7.5, plus a long tail - roughly 180 impressions, one click, of people looking for bio COPY to write about themselves. They do not want a page builder. Meanwhile the query that actually describes the product, 'link in bio for real estate agents', gets 28 impressions at position 21.18, and 'link in bio for realtors' 4 at 28.25. The site is on page 3 for what it sells and page 9 for what it does not. Retarget the homepage at the commercial query; US-155 handles the informational cluster separately so it is captured rather than abandoned.
acceptanceCriteria: The homepage <title>, meta description, og:title and H1 target the 'link in bio for real estate agents' / 'link in bio for realtors' intent and no longer lead with 'real estate agent bio'
index.html's hardcoded fallback title and description are updated to match, so the shell and the hydrated page agree
The change is made in one place - the homepage SEO source - and index.html's fallback derives from it or is documented as needing to be kept in step
H1 and title are consistent with each other and with the page's actual first screen of copy
og:image and twitter card still resolve to a real file
Typecheck passes: tsc --noEmit succeeds
userStories.notes: Depends on US-147 (a title change is worthless while every URL shares one title). Expect impressions to FALL and clicks to rise - the 180 wrong-intent impressions are noise and losing them is the point. Record the pre-change baseline in progress.txt (33 clicks / 1,481 impressions / position 18.4 over the 16 months to 2026-09-08) so the next runner can tell improvement from drift. Do not also change the brand name; that is not this story. Single source is src/config/homepage-seo.ts; a homepage-seo transformIndexHtml plugin in vite.config.ts writes the same strings into index.html at build time. Found two hero defects on the way: HeroSection split the H1 on its last two words (would have rendered 'Link in Bio for Real' / 'Estate Agents'), fixed with an explicit titleHighlight prop; and HeroSectionLazy's fallback hardcoded the old headline and ignored every text prop, contradicting the title on slow connections and on all five /features/* pages. Gradient text on the hero H1 is a pre-existing craft-floor violation, flagged but deliberately not changed.

userStories.title: Gate the 23 thin /for/{city} pages behind noindex until they carry something a Miami agent could not get from the Austin page
userStories.description: A risk that US-147 creates rather than removes. The 23 /for/{city}-real-estate-agents pages are generated from LOCATIONS in src/data/locations.ts by a single 715-line LocationTemplate.tsx; each differs only by city name, a median price, an agent count, a one-sentence marketDescription and a neighbourhood list. Today that is harmless because none of them has ever been crawled well enough to receive a single impression in 16 months. The moment prerendering makes them real, 23 near-identical pages enter the index at once on a domain with almost no authority, which is the classic doorway-page pattern and a site-wide quality risk. Ship them noindexed, and let a page earn its way in.
acceptanceCriteria: /for/{slug} pages are prerendered (so they are crawlable and their directives visible) but emit noindex, follow by default
A per-location flag in src/data/locations.ts controls indexability, defaulting to off, so a city page can be switched on individually once it has real content
Documented criteria for switching one on - what 'real content' means here (genuinely local, verifiable, not template-substituted) - written into docs/seo/ and referenced from the data file
Noindexed city pages are excluded from sitemap.xml; a page switched on is included automatically
At most 2 city pages are switched on as worked examples, and only if they are given substantive unique content in this story
Typecheck passes: tsc --noEmit succeeds
userStories.notes: Depends on US-147 and US-149. This is deliberately conservative and will feel like a step backwards - it is not. 23 templated pages ranking nowhere cost nothing; 23 templated pages indexed on a weak domain can cost the pages that matter. Do not delete the pages or the data; the template is fine and the approach becomes viable once the domain has authority. ZERO cities switched on, deliberately: the criterion allowed up to two 'only if they are given substantive unique content', and writing verifiable local market claims without a source would be fabrication - the exact thing docs/seo/CITY_PAGES.md rule 1 forbids. The flag was proven in both directions (Miami temporarily flipped to indexable, rebuilt, appeared in the sitemap with index,follow, then reverted). The first real city page is a content task for someone who knows that market.

userStories.title: Consolidate 25 near-duplicate blog posts into four guides
userStories.description: The blog is one topic written 25 times. From the GSC page report: 'the-ultimate-guide-to-link-ideas-for-real-estate-pages', 'the-smart-agent-s-guide-to-creating-a-link-for-home-tours', 'instagram-link-ideas-for-realtors', 'home-sales-link-ideas', 'agent-click-page-tips', 'agent-qr-code-setup-ideas', 'home-selling-link-hub', 'home-ads-link-hub', 'agent-core-link-setup', 'best-contact-link-buttons', 'the-complete-agent-link-hub-guide', 'link-hub-for-leasing-agents', 'agent-page-link-ideas', 'link-hub-for-listings', 'link-hub-for-top-agents', 'how-agents-send-links-online', 'agent-call-link-layout', 'the-landlord-agent-link-page', 'how-agents-get-leads-from-social-bio-links', 'how-to-link-your-active-listings', 'why-every-real-estate-agent-needs-an-online-resume-page', and more - all permutations of agent + link + hub/page/ideas. Together they earned 2 clicks in 16 months. This is the pattern Google's helpful-content signals demote site-wide, so it is plausibly suppressing the pages that matter. One post is genuinely working and must be preserved: how-real-estate-agents-use-link-in-bio-to-generate-more-leads-in-2024 at 162 impressions, 6 clicks, position 11.09 - 18% of all site clicks.
acceptanceCriteria: The permutation posts are merged into at most four substantial guides, each answering a distinct question rather than a distinct keyword phrasing
how-real-estate-agents-use-link-in-bio-to-generate-more-leads-in-2024 is kept at its existing URL, expanded rather than merged away, and its '2024' framing refreshed without changing the slug
Every retired slug 301s to the guide that absorbed it - implemented in public/_redirects (Cloudflare Pages), not as a client-side redirect, so the signal actually passes
No retired URL returns the SPA NotFound page: assert every 301 source resolves to a 200 at its target
No redirect chains: every source points directly at its final target
Retired slugs are removed from sitemap.xml and the surviving guides are present with correct lastmod
The articles rows for retired posts are unpublished rather than deleted, so the content is recoverable
Internal links pointing at retired slugs are updated to the surviving guides
Typecheck passes: tsc --noEmit succeeds
userStories.notes: Depends on US-148 and US-149. Pruning feels destructive and is the single most reliable site-wide quality move available here. Get the redirect map right in one pass - a chain of 301s or a redirect into a 404 is worse than leaving the post up. Write the full old-slug -> new-slug map into progress.txt before making any change. BLOCKED 2026-09-08, passes stays false. The map is written up in docs/seo/BLOG_CONSOLIDATION.md (one kept pillar plus four proposed guides, all 26 retired slugs assigned, no chains) and the safety check is built and proven: verifyServedLayout() in scripts/prerender.mts now fails the build on a 301 whose target is not a page the build produced, and on a 301 into another 301 - both demonstrated against the real build, with a legitimate redirect still passing. Criteria 4 and 5 are therefore done. Criteria 1, 2, 6 and 7 need production: merging 27 posts requires reading them, and their bodies exist only in the articles table (no seed migration, no fixture, no copy in the repo). Redirects were deliberately NOT added - shipping them before the guides exist would 301 26 currently-working URLs into 404s. Execute in the documented order: write and publish the guides, then redirect, then unpublish the old rows, then rebuild. Also found: two dead internal links in src/lib/geo.ts (/blog/instagram-marketing-for-real-estate and /compare), unrelated to this consolidation - for US-124 or US-156.

userStories.title: A real estate agent bio generator, to capture the 180-impression cluster the homepage currently fails
userStories.description: Rather than abandon the wrong-intent traffic US-152 stops chasing, serve it. 'real estate agent bio' (82 impressions, position 88.56), 'professional real estate agent bio examples' (position 7.5), 'real estate bio for new agents', 'real estate agent bio for new agents', 'luxury real estate agent bio', 'realtor instagram bio', 'real estate bio generator' - roughly 180 impressions across 16 months with no page built for them at all, ranking on the homepage's title alone. The infrastructure already exists: src/lib/instagram-bio-analyzer/ and src/lib/listing-description-generator/ are shipped free tools with routes at /tools/instagram-bio-analyzer and /tools/listing-description-generator. This is the same shape, and it feeds the funnel honestly - here is your bio, now where does the link in it point?
acceptanceCriteria: A free bio tool ships at a route under /tools/ following the pattern of the two existing tools (structure, layout and lead-capture behaviour consistent with them)
It produces a usable bio without an account, and covers the intents the query data actually shows: new agent, luxury, rental/leasing, team, and Instagram-length
Real worked examples are on the page as crawlable text, not generated only on interaction - the examples are what can rank
The page is prerendered with its own title, description, canonical and appropriate schema, and is in the sitemap
It converts: a clear, non-obnoxious path from finished bio to creating a page, measured with the existing analytics
No new heavyweight dependency; reuse the existing tool scaffolding and UI components
The page respects the UI craft floor in CLAUDE.md - run `npx impeccable detect` on the new files and address what it flags
Typecheck passes: tsc --noEmit succeeds
userStories.notes: Depends on US-147. Read src/lib/instagram-bio-analyzer/ first and follow it rather than inventing a second pattern. If the tool needs an LLM call, route it through an edge function - no API key in the bundle. This story and US-152 are a pair: one stops the homepage chasing the query, the other builds the page that deserves it. Deterministic templates, no model call and no new dependency - src/lib/agent-bio-generator/ mirrors the existing instagram-bio-analyzer shape. The five worked examples are generated by the generator itself at module load so they cannot drift from it, and all five are present in the built HTML. Analytics via the existing gtag pattern rather than a new Supabase table, which would need a migration this machine cannot verify. impeccable clean on the new page.

userStories.title: /vs/linktree is the highest commercial intent page in the category and it has never had an impression
userStories.description: The three comparison pages - /vs/linktree, /vs/beacons, /vs/later - are routed (App.tsx) and in the sitemap, and have zero impressions across the full 16 months. US-147 makes them visible; this story makes them worth finding. Comparison queries are where someone with a credit card out ends up, and 'linktree alternative for real estate agents' is the exact query this product should own. Currently the roundup articles owning those SERPs do not mention AgentBio at all.
acceptanceCriteria: /vs/linktree is built out as a substantive, honest comparison: a real feature matrix, pricing reality, and a clear statement of who Linktree is genuinely better for - a comparison that only wins is not credible and does not convert
Claims about the competitor are accurate as of the build date and dated on the page, so they can be maintained
/vs/beacons and /vs/later are brought to the same standard or reduced to one page, rather than left as three thin variants (the US-153 lesson)
Each comparison page is prerendered with its own title, description, canonical and FAQ/Product schema where genuinely applicable, and appears in the sitemap
Comparison pages are reachable from the pricing page and the primary navigation, not orphaned
Comparison tables scroll horizontally on mobile rather than forcing the page to - 81% of the site's impressions are desktop but mobile CTR is already higher (3.32% vs 2.00%)
The pages respect the UI craft floor in CLAUDE.md - `npx impeccable detect` clean or justified
Typecheck passes: tsc --noEmit succeeds
userStories.notes: Depends on US-147. Do not publish comparison claims you have not checked - a stale or wrong pricing table on a competitor is both a credibility and a legal problem. Put the check date in the page copy and in a constant, so the next runner knows when it went stale. Found and removed five fabricated testimonials (two on /vs/linktree, three on /vs/beacons including a $2.4M closed-volume claim), all hardcoded rather than from the testimonials table. Fixed two contradictions about our OWN price ($39 vs $49 on one page; $19 vs $29 on another; neither $39 nor $19 is a plan). Competitor prices removed entirely and deliberately: linktr.ee shows pricing in local currency by region and warns tiers change, so no single USD figure is honest - src/config/competitors.ts holds tier names plus an honest betterWhen list, dated COMPETITORS_VERIFIED_ON=2026-09-08 and rendered on the page. Pages were orphaned; now linked from the footer and the pricing FAQ. SITE-WIDE: seven more hardcoded testimonials remain outside this story's scope - see progress.txt.

userStories.title: Rich results: the whole site produced 3 Product-snippet impressions in 16 months
userStories.description: Search appearance for the entire 16-month window: 'Product snippets, 0 clicks, 3 impressions'. That is the sum of the site's structured-data presence. The components exist - src/components/seo/SchemaMarkup.tsx, src/components/ReviewSchema.tsx, src/components/Breadcrumbs.tsx, src/components/seo/Breadcrumb.tsx and the schema prop on SEOHead - and like everything else they only run after hydration, so a crawler collecting rich-result eligibility never sees them. Once US-147 puts them in the served HTML, make the coverage deliberate.
acceptanceCriteria: SoftwareApplication (or Product) schema with offers on the homepage and /pricing, matching the real plans in subscription_plans rather than the pricing-plans.ts copy
Article schema on every blog post with author, datePublished and dateModified taken from the articles row
BreadcrumbList on blog posts, /features/*, /vs/* and /for/* - the components already exist, wire them consistently
FAQPage only where a real FAQ is visible on the page, never as invisible markup
Organization/WebSite schema once, sitewide, with a single sameAs set
Every emitted block validates: the US-150 verify:seo check parses each JSON-LD block and fails on invalid or contradictory markup
No schema describes content that is not visible on the page - that is a manual-action risk, not a shortcut
Typecheck passes: tsc --noEmit succeeds
userStories.notes: Depends on US-147 and US-150. subscription_plans is the enforced matrix and pricing-plans.ts is copy (see the constraints noted for US-128..US-143) - schema must follow the enforced source or it will advertise prices the app will not honour. Review schema needs real reviews; do not emit aggregateRating from seeded or sample testimonials. Found invented star ratings (4.8 from 523 reviews) live on 31 pages from five sources US-111 missed - now 0. Found the phantom $39 price in five places, one of them attached to a node named Professional which costs 49; all now derive from PRICING_PLANS, and the homepage Offer became an AggregateOffer 29-299. Found 18 FAQ questions marked up but not visible across six pages; FaqSection.tsx now produces the schema and the visible list from one array so they cannot drift. verify:seo now parses every JSON-LD block and was proven to fail on malformed JSON, on a reinstated 4.8/523, and on an invisible FAQ question. No Review or aggregateRating schema added anywhere.

userStories.title: The uncomfortable one: position 18-20 on every page regardless of topic is a domain with no links
userStories.description: Across 16 months the site averages position 18.39 on desktop and 20.40 on mobile, and the average barely moves by page or by topic - /pricing 4.77 and a handful of blog posts at 3-6 are the exceptions, and even those convert nothing. Uniform mid-page-two ranking irrespective of content quality is the signature of a domain with essentially no authority. US-147 through US-157 will move pages from roughly position 20 to roughly position 10; they cannot move them to 1-5. What does is being present in the 'best link in bio tools for realtors' roundups that currently own those SERPs, and in the directories real estate agents actually consult. That work is human outreach, but the assets it requires and the target list it needs are buildable, and their absence is what stalls it.
acceptanceCriteria: A researched, prioritised link-acquisition target list committed to docs/seo/ - the roundup articles currently ranking for 'link in bio for real estate agents', 'linktree alternative for realtors' and neighbouring queries, plus the real estate tech directories, review platforms (G2, Capterra) and agent communities, each with the actual submission or contact route and an effort/likelihood note

The on-site assets a roundup author needs in order to include the product: a press/about page with accurate positioning, logo files in usable formats, a plain-language feature summary and screenshots, at a stable URL
Outreach templates that are specific enough to send - one for a roundup author, one for a directory submission, one for a partnership approach - with the honest pitch, not a generic mail merge
A single owner-facing checklist in docs/seo/ describing what is a code task and what is a human task here, so the next runner does not silently no-op the human half
Nothing in this story fabricates a placement, a review, or a directory listing, and no template asks anyone else to
Typecheck passes: tsc --noEmit succeeds
userStories.notes: Last, and mostly not a coding task - it is here so it is not forgotten, and the story is scoped to the artifacts an agent can honestly produce. Do NOT attempt to acquire links, create accounts, post to communities or contact anyone; produce the list, the assets and the templates and stop. Say plainly in progress.txt that the outreach itself is outstanding and belongs to a person. Research changed the plan: the money-query SERP is dominated by COMPETITOR-owned listicles (linqin, simplelistings, direct.me, clientkeeper, linkship), which are not link targets. Real targets are HousingWire, The Close and Inman - every Tier 1 URL actually retrieved 2026-09-08. Tier 2/3 listed as categories with their submission routes explicitly marked unverified. /press ships with only checkable facts, prices read from PRICING_PLANS, and no counts, funding, awards, ratings or testimonials; screenshots deliberately absent rather than invented. NOBODY WAS CONTACTED, no account created, no listing submitted, no placement claimed - that half is human and is item 7 of docs/seo/SEO_RECOVERY_CHECKLIST.md, gated behind removing the seven remaining fabricated testimonials. Also fixed a real regression: routes.test.ts treated static assets like /logo.png as broken routes.

userStories.title: Remove every fabricated testimonial and unverifiable claim from the marketing UI
userStories.description: Third pass at the same defect, authorised by Dj on 2026-09-08. US-111 found the signup page saying '2,500+ agents' while the landing page said '5,000+', plus an invented ratingValue 4.8 over 523 reviews in the JSON-LD, and fixed what it saw. US-156 found five hardcoded testimonials on the comparison pages, one carrying '$2.4M closed from Instagram'. US-157 found that same 4.8/523 rating still live on 31 pages from five sources US-111 had missed. This pass swept the whole of src/ and found: FIVE different invented agent counts (2,847, 4,200+, 2,000+, 3,000+, 10,000+, plus the original 5,000+ still live on two landing pages), a hardcoded '4.9/5 rating' in two capture modals and a '4.9/5 Agent Rating' stat, 'Used by agents at Keller Williams, Coldwell Banker, RE/MAX' naming three real firms as customers, '2,847+ Agents Analyzed' / '3X Average Lead Increase' / '$50M+ In Deals Generated', eight more named testimonials across the tools pages, a templated 'Success Stories from {city} Agents' block rendering two fictional agents on all 26 city pages, a four-testimonial 'Agent Success Stories' section on /vs/later, and an email drip quoting invented percentile benchmarks and 'Real results from {market} agents: Agent A: 3 leads/month -> 18 leads/month' to real inboxes.
acceptanceCriteria: No named testimonial is hardcoded in the UI. Real ones come from the `testimonials` table with consent recorded, rendered like every other testimonial
No customer, user or agent count appears unless something can produce it. MARKETING_COPY.joinLine from src/config/marketing-claims.ts is the honest placeholder
No star rating we did not receive. Ratings computed from real testimonials (ReviewSchema, FullProfilePage) are untouched
No other company is named as a customer
No outcome metric (leads/month, closings, in sales, X increase) is claimed without measurement
The email drip contains no invented case studies, benchmarks or trust statistics
A test fails the build if any of these return - src/marketing-claims.test.ts, with an allowlist that names each legitimate exception and why
The guard is demonstrated able to fail, not merely to pass
npm run build, tsc --noEmit and npm run verify:seo all pass
userStories.notes: Authorised explicitly by Dj: 'No fabricated text, we need to remove false claims and false testimonies.' Nothing was reworded into a vaguer version of the same claim - a claim either has something behind it or it went. Deliberately KEPT, with reasons recorded in the test's ALLOWED_FILES: the BioAnalyzerForm dropdown asking a visitor about their own current leads; the 'Keller Williams, Coldwell Banker, etc.' placeholder in a 'your brokerage' input; features/Testimonials describing the star-display feature ('4.8/5.0, 4.9/5.0, etc.'); the ExampleBio demos and the bio-generator's suggested sample credentials, which are illustrations of what an agent might write about themselves rather than claims about us; and Zapier's own published '5,000+ apps' figure. Verified against the built output as well as source: a 248-file scan of dist/ for 24 banned strings comes back with only coincidental matches (SVG path data, MD5 constants) and the legitimate feature description.

userStories.title: Stop deploying 17 MB of source maps that publish the entire TypeScript source
userStories.description: vite.config.ts set `sourcemap: 'hidden'` unconditionally, with the comment "These are hidden source maps that won't expose source code to users". That is not what 'hidden' does. It omits the `//# sourceMappingURL=` comment from the bundle so a browser will not fetch the map on its own; the .map files are still written into dist/ and still deployed. The URL is derivable from any chunk name visible in the network tab, so `https://agentbio.net/assets/index-<hash>.js.map` returned the whole source. 193 maps, 17 MB, 71% of a 24 MB deploy — every query shape, every RLS assumption and every unshipped route, public. The stated justification was Sentry symbolication, but nothing consumed them: there is no @sentry/vite-plugin and no upload step in .github/workflows. US-125 reduced this and did not close it.
acceptanceCriteria: A default `npm run build` writes no .map file into dist/.
BUILD_SOURCEMAPS=true still emits hidden maps, for a local analyze run or a CI job that uploads to an error tracker and deletes them before deploy.
scripts/check-bundle-size.mjs (the CI `size-check` job) fails when a .map reaches dist/assets without that flag set.
The misleading comment in vite.config.ts is replaced with what 'hidden' actually does.
userStories.notes: Done 2026-09-09. dist drops 24 MB -> 6.4 MB. Both paths verified against a real build: default emits 0 maps, BUILD_SOURCEMAPS=true emits 193, and the guard was demonstrated failing by dropping one .map into dist/assets.

userStories.title: The UI has 65 machine-detectable AI-generated-design tells
userStories.description: `npx impeccable detect src` reports 65 anti-patterns across the app: 49 ai-color-palette (purple/violet gradients — InstagramBioAnalyzer and ListingDescriptionGenerator are the worst, but Landing, Pricing, Login, Register and LocationTemplate all carry them), 10 gradient-text on headings, 3 side-tab, 1 overused-font, 1 gray-on-color and 1 border-accent-on-rounded. CLAUDE.md names every one of these as a category default to refuse. This is not a lint fix: removing a purple gradient means deciding what replaces it, so it needs a palette and type decision first and then a page-by-page pass. Multi-iteration by nature.
acceptanceCriteria: A single documented palette and type scale exists, chosen deliberately rather than inherited from the shadcn default.
`npx impeccable detect src` reports zero gradient-text and zero ai-color-palette findings.
The remaining side-tab, overused-font, gray-on-color and border-accent-on-rounded findings are each fixed or recorded with a reason.
A CI check runs the detector so the count cannot silently climb back.
userStories.notes: Opened 2026-09-09 during the platform-improvement loop. Take the palette/type decision first in one iteration, then the two tools pages (16 of the 49 palette findings sit in those two files), then the rest.

userStories.title: The Leads page downloaded 605 KB of PDF library to render an Export CSV button
userStories.description: src/lib/exportUtils.ts opened with `import { jsPDF } from 'jspdf'` at the top. It also exports exportToCSV, which is a string builder and a Blob download and has nothing to do with PDF. src/pages/dashboard/Leads.tsx imports exportToCSV and nothing else from that module — but a top-level import makes the jspdf chunk a static dependency of every consumer, and Rollup cannot tree-shake it because generatePDFReport in the same module genuinely uses it. Verified in the built output: Leads -> exportUtils (3 KB) -> export-vendor (605 KB / 184 KB gzip), all on the critical path of the most-visited page in a lead-generation CRM. Two knock-on defects came out of the same manualChunks entry: 'html2canvas' was listed in it and is not a dependency of this project at all, and naming jspdf there made Rollup place Vite's __vitePreload helper inside the resulting chunk, so consumers statically imported 605 KB to get a 200-byte function. This is also why `npm run size-check` was red on main: export-vendor was 605 KB against a 600 KB vendor budget.
acceptanceCriteria: jsPDF and jspdf-autotable are loaded with a dynamic import inside the PDF functions, not at module top level.
The built Leads chunk has no static import of any jspdf chunk.
The PDF call sites await the now-async functions, so the success toast follows the download and a failure is reported rather than becoming an unhandled rejection.
A test asserts on the source that no top-level jspdf import has come back.
`npm run size-check` passes.
userStories.notes: Done 2026-09-09. export-vendor no longer exists: jspdf is a 386 KB async chunk plus a 31 KB autotable chunk, fetched on click. Verified in dist, not inferred.

userStories.title: Every page loaded 800 KB of Three.js it never rendered
userStories.description: Vite's __vitePreload helper is a virtual module with no home of its own, so Rollup files it into whichever manualChunks group it likes. It had landed in three-vendor. Every chunk that lazy-loads anything therefore emitted `import{_}from"./three-vendor-<hash>.js"` — a STATIC import of an 800 KB chunk to obtain a 200-byte function. The story was opened believing FullProfilePage (/:username, the page every agent puts in their Instagram bio) was the victim. Writing the guard showed it was worse: the ENTRY chunk index-*.js was a static importer too, so every visitor to every route on the platform — landing page included — downloaded 800 KB / 220 KB gzip of Three.js before first paint, whether or not anything on the page rendered 3D. Before US-162 the helper lived in the jspdf chunk and the same importers paid 605 KB for that instead, so this has been true continuously; only the victim changed. It also made the exception in scripts/check-bundle-size.mjs — three-vendor is "lazy-loaded only on 3D hero sections, never on first paint" — false, and nothing noticed, because the exception carried only prose.
acceptanceCriteria: The __vitePreload helper lives in react-vendor, which every page loads anyway, not in a lazy vendor chunk.
Only the 3D components themselves statically import three-vendor.
Neither the entry chunk nor FullProfilePage has three-vendor in its static import graph.
The bundle-size exception names the chunks allowed to statically import it, and the check enforces that — prose alone could not catch this.
The chunk name set and vendor chunk sizes are unchanged, so the manualChunks rewrite reshuffled nothing.
userStories.notes: Done 2026-09-09. manualChunks converted from the object form to a function, because the object form resolves its entries as package specifiers and cannot name a virtual module — `'vite/preload-helper'` in the react-vendor array kills the build with `Missing "./preload-helper" specifier in "vite" package`. Verified against real builds: identical 195-chunk name set before and after, vendor sizes within 6 KB, and the new guard demonstrated failing against the old config — where it named four static importers including the entry chunk.

userStories.title: A 394 KB charting library was on the landing page's critical path, to supply clsx
userStories.description: With three-vendor off the critical path (US-163), the entry chunk still statically imported charts-vendor — 394 KB of recharts, in a chunk whose own comment reads "Charts - dashboard only". Every visitor to the marketing landing page, every blog reader and every public profile visitor paid for it. It was not a stray chart component: all six recharts importers are admin or dashboard and correctly lazy. The entry pulled exactly one binding, and it was clsx — the `twMerge(clsx(inputs))` inside cn() in src/lib/utils.ts, which every component in the app calls. clsx has no assigned home in VENDOR_CHUNKS, recharts happens to depend on it, so Rollup filed it into charts-vendor and the entry imported the whole chunk to get a 500-byte function. @babel/runtime's helpers had been adopted the same way, which is why three-vendor also imported charts-vendor: loading a 3D profile theme pulled in recharts to get Object.assign. This is US-163's defect one layer down — a tiny shared module with no home is adopted by whichever large chunk happens to want it, and every consumer pays for the whole thing. It is invisible in a chunk listing, because the sizes all look fine.
acceptanceCriteria: clsx, tailwind-merge, class-variance-authority and @babel/runtime are named in VENDOR_CHUNKS so they land in react-vendor, which every page loads anyway.
The built entry chunk has no static import of charts-vendor.
charts-vendor is statically imported only by dashboard and admin chunks.
three-vendor no longer statically imports charts-vendor.
The bundle-size check enforces this for charts-vendor as well as three-vendor, and the enforcement is demonstrated failing against the old config.
userStories.notes: Done 2026-09-09. Entry static vendor imports are now form, react, state, supabase, ui — no charts. react-vendor grows 161.5 -> 184.3 KB, which is the four utility packages moving into a chunk that was already loaded, against 394 KB leaving the critical path. The check's staticImporters idea from US-163 was generalised into MUST_STAY_LAZY, covering three-vendor and charts-vendor and independent of whether a chunk is over budget. Demonstrated failing against the pre-fix config, where it named both the entry chunk and three-vendor.

userStories.title: A blog category outside BlogCategory's hardcoded map fails the render gate and breaks the entire build
userStories.description: scripts/lib/articles.mts categorySlugs() derives /blog/category/{slug} routes from whatever string sits in articles.category, slugified. src/pages/BlogCategory.tsx renders from categoryContent, a hardcoded Record keyed by nine slugs. A published article whose category is anything else produces a prerender route with no content: the page keeps index.html's default title and emits no canonical, prerender.mts refuses to write ANY file, and `npm run build` exits 1. An editor changing one dropdown value in the CMS takes the deploy down, and the failure message talks about titles rather than about the category.
acceptanceCriteria: A category present on a published article but absent from BlogCategory's map does not fail the build

The behaviour is decided deliberately: either the category page renders generic-but-real content from the articles themselves, or the route is not generated at all and the articles still appear under /blog
Whichever is chosen, a test covers an article with an unknown category
If a route is skipped, it is skipped in sitemap generation too — no URL is advertised for a page that does not exist
A prerendered /blog/category/{slug} page lists only articles in that category
userStories.notes: Done 2026-09-10, iteration 2 of the SEO loop. The two sources of truth are now one: src/config/blog-categories.ts, plain data with no React import so scripts/lib/articles.mts can read it from node. categorySlugs() returns only categories that have a page AND a published article, plus an `unlisted` list the prerender prints — loud, not fatal, and not silent either. categoryContent in BlogCategory.tsx is now Record<BlogCategorySlug, ...>, so the other direction of drift (a registry entry with no copy written for it) is a tsc error in the file that has to supply it. Two further defects were found and fixed in the same pass: the prerender's articles intercept ignored the category filter, so every prerendered category page listed every published article regardless of category (verified against a real dist before and after); and an article's category was a bare badge, so nothing led from a post to the other posts on its topic — it links now, and only when the category actually has a page.

userStories.title: There is no /tools hub, so the free-tools breadcrumbs claim a level that does not exist
userStories.description: All three tool pages render a Breadcrumb whose middle item is called 'Free Tools' and points at /tools/instagram-bio-analyzer — a sibling tool, not a hub. There is no /tools route in App.tsx. The BreadcrumbList JSON-LD therefore asserts a hierarchy the site does not have, and the three tools have no shared parent page to collect the topical relevance between them. US-165 linked the tools from the footer, which fixes reachability but not the missing hub.
acceptanceCriteria: /tools exists as a route, is prerendered, is in the sitemap and passes verify:seo
It lists the three tools with a real description of each, not a grid of identical cards
Every tool page's breadcrumb middle item points at /tools
The footer's 'Free tools' column heading links to it
userStories.notes: Done 2026-09-10, iteration 3 of the SEO loop, together with US-168. /tools exists, is prerendered, is in the sitemap and reads src/config/tools.ts — the same registry the footer's Free tools column renders, so a tool cannot be added to one and forgotten in the other, which is how the bio generator became US-165. The /features hub was NOT built: rather than invent a thin page, /features/lead-capture's breadcrumb dropped the rung it could not honour. US-171 is the open question of whether a real features hub earns its place.

userStories.title: InstagramBioAnalyzer's breadcrumb is built from window.location.origin and repeats its own URL
userStories.description: src/pages/tools/InstagramBioAnalyzer.tsx passes { name: 'Home', url: window.location.origin } and then gives both the 'Free Tools' item and the 'Instagram Bio Analyzer' item the same URL, /tools/instagram-bio-analyzer. AgentBioGenerator.tsx next door uses getCanonicalUrl() for exactly the same three items. The origin form is what put http://127.0.0.1:4319 into canonicals before US-147 rewrote it out of every snapshot, so the JSON-LD here survives only because of that rewrite.
acceptanceCriteria: The breadcrumb items use getCanonicalUrl(), matching AgentBioGenerator.tsx

userStories.title: Every canonical on the site was whatever host served the page
userStories.description: getBaseUrl() in seo.config.ts was getSafeOrigin(), which in a browser is window.location.origin, and roughly thirty call sites built canonicals, og:url and JSON-LD url/@id from window.location.origin directly. Every site-owned page therefore declared itself canonical at whichever host served it. On agentbio.net that is right by coincidence. Cloudflare Pages gives every branch a *.pages.dev preview URL serving the whole site: the prerendered HTML carries the correct canonical because prerender.mts rewrites its own preview origin out of every snapshot, but react-helmet-async overwrites it with the pages.dev host the moment the bundle hydrates, and Googlebot renders JavaScript. A canonical is a claim about identity and cannot be a reading of the current environment.
acceptanceCriteria: getBaseUrl() returns the configured app URL, not the visitor's host
No file in the SEO layer builds a URL from window.location.origin or getSafeOrigin
getSafeOrigin stays where the visitor's host IS canonical — /:username and /p/:slug, which a tenant may serve from a custom domain — and each such call site says why
A test proves the canonical is unchanged when the page is served from a *.pages.dev host
A test fails if the pattern is reintroduced anywhere in the SEO layer
The prerender reports how many preview-server URLs it had to rewrite, rather than silently papering over them
userStories.notes: Done 2026-09-10, iteration 4 of the SEO loop. Bigger than the story as written in iteration 3, which framed it as tidiness: the point is not that a helper exists, it is that a preview deploy could self-canonicalise the entire site. The prerender's origin rewrite turned out to be silently loadbearing, so it now counts and reports what it moved. Measured against real builds: 671 preview-server URLs across all 58 pages before, 0 after. The counter earned its place immediately — after the first sweep it still found 7 on the homepage, which the sweep had missed. Stripe return URLs, OAuth redirectTo and the dashboard's copy-your-link UI keep window.location.origin deliberately: those want the host the user is actually on.

Close deals 30% faster.'; /vs/later said '3-5x higher conversion rates' five times, including in its meta description and in a FAQPage answer Google renders as a rich result; the dashboard insights widget told agents 'profiles with property listings get 3x more leads' and 'agents with 5+ listings convert 40% better'; /features/testimonials said video testimonials are '10x more powerful than text'; the email drip's subject line was 'The Instagram bio mistake 73% of agents make'. Separately, US-159 deleted the names under three quotes on the listing generator and left the quotes, and its attribution rule wanted an em-dash, so two named testimonials on /features/calendar-booking — 'Jessica T., Luxury Agent, Scottsdale AZ' and 'Marcus L., Team Leader, Denver CO' — were never touched.

The new rules earned their place on the first run: they found two claims inside the bio analyzer's scoring output that no reading had spotted — 'AgentBio captures 3X more leads than Linktree for agents', an unsubstantiated comparative claim about a named competitor delivered as the tool's own advice, and 'top performers in your area score 50+ points higher, which translates to 3-5X more leads', which invents both a local benchmark and a conversion rate for a deterministic six-check rubric. userStories.title: og:image declared a size no code had ever measured
userStories.description: Four SEO components hardcoded og:image:width 1200 and og:image:height 630 beside the URL. Cover.png is 1536x1024 — a 1.5 aspect ratio where the tags claim 1.905 — so 52 of 58 pages told every unfurl to reserve a shape the image does not have. userStories.title: Every URL on the site returned 200, and the body it returned was the homepage
userStories.description: public/_redirects ended in `/* /index.html 200`. Since US-147 dist/index.html is not an empty shell — it is the fully prerendered homepage — so agentbio.net/anything-at-all answered 200 with the homepage's title, description, canonical and body, and only became the 404 page after the bundle executed and React Router matched `*`. A client-side router cannot set a status code, so nothing in NotFound.tsx could have fixed it. The effect was an infinite URL space in which every typo, every retired link and every path a crawler invented returned a duplicate of the homepage under a 200. The single-segment case is worse than the rest: /:username is indistinguishable from a typo without a database lookup, and functions/[username].ts already performed that lookup — then called next() either way, so a crawler asking for a handle that does not exist got the homepage.
acceptanceCriteria: An unknown URL under a prefix whose real URLs are all prerendered returns 404 with the 404 document
dist/404.html exists and is what Cloudflare Pages serves for an unmatched request
Every route App.tsx defines is either prerendered or covered by a rule, and a test enforces both directions
A crawler requesting an unpublished or nonexistent username gets 404, while a failed database lookup still falls through to the SPA
The 404 page carries its own title and a noindex, and links somewhere
userStories.notes: Done 2026-09-10, iteration 7 of the SEO loop. The risky part is _redirects: deleting the catch-all turns any route that is neither prerendered nor listed into a broken page, and Cloudflare Pages routing cannot be exercised in this sandbox. src/spa-routes.test.ts is what stands in for a deploy — it walks App.tsx and _redirects and asserts they agree in both directions, and was demonstrated failing by deleting the /admin rules. Note the deliberate asymmetry in the Pages Function: `profiles === null` (the lookup errored or timed out) still falls through, because answering 404 there would turn a database blip into a deindexing event for every agent at once; only an empty array — PostgREST answering that there is no such profile — produces a 404. A second defect surfaced while verifying: the US-174 og:image rule, on its first run against a full build, found three pages shipping no og:image at all — /vs/later, /tools/instagram-bio-analyzer and /tools/listing-description-generator, each building its own <Helmet> with no og:* tags, while the static twitter:* tags from index.html survived still describing the homepage. Fixed in the same commit. The mechanism by which the static og:* tags vanish while the static twitter:* ones remain was not established; the fix does not depend on it, but it is an open observation.

userStories.title: llms.txt still carried the invented figures three sweeps removed from the UI, and linked to four pages that do not exist

A test enforces all of the above and is demonstrated failing on the file as it shipped
userStories.notes: Done 2026-09-10, iteration 8 of the SEO loop. 7 of the 8 checks fail on the shipped file. Worth noting how it survived three cleanups: it is a text file in public/, so a sweep of src/ never reaches it, and it is not rendered by any component, so no page audit sees it either. The distinction the lead-volume rule had to learn: '100 leads a month' on a pricing line is a limit the product enforces, while 'the average user captures 10+ qualified leads a month' is a claim about outcomes. Only the second is banned, and getting that wrong first made the test fail on the honest rewrite it existed to protect. A `[\d,]+` pattern also matched the bare comma in 'agents, realtors' — every count pattern now requires a digit.

userStories.title: The Organization schema claimed six social accounts, and the site links four different ones
userStories.description: schema.org sameAs on an Organization is a claim of identity — these accounts ARE this organisation — and it is what Google reconciles an entity against when building a knowledge panel. Two sameAs lists shipped on every page, from src/lib/seo.ts and src/components/seo/PageSEO.tsx, plus a third copy in SEO_CONFIG.socialLinks, all naming twitter.com/agentbio, facebook.com/agentbio, linkedin.com/company/agentbio, instagram.com/agentbio, youtube.com/@agentbio and github.com/agentbio. The footer links facebook.com/agentbioapp, x.com/AgentBioApp, instagram.com/agentbioapp and linkedin.com/company/agentbio. Only LinkedIn is in both. So the site told Google it owned four accounts under a handle it does not use, and asserted a YouTube channel and a GitHub organisation that appear nowhere else in the repository. SEO_CONFIG.twitterHandle was '@agentbio' for the same reason, so twitter:site and twitter:creator named a different account on every page. Separately, SEO_CONFIG.organization declared logoWidth 512 and logoHeight 512 and both Organization schemas shipped logo ImageObject width '512' height '512'; public/logo.png is 946x436, which is the US-174 defect again in the node that says who the company is.
acceptanceCriteria: One list of social profiles, with the bar for inclusion written down: the site links to it
The footer, both sameAs lists, SEO_CONFIG.socialLinks, twitter:site and llms.txt all read that list
Organization.logo declares the size logo.png actually is, verified against the file
A test fails if any of them names an account that is not in the list, demonstrated against the code as it shipped
userStories.notes: Done 2026-09-10, iteration 9 of the SEO loop. Six checks fail on the shipped code. The bar for inclusion is 'the footer links to it', because that is the only evidence available in this repository that an account exists and is ours — claiming an account you do not own is worse than omitting one you do, since an omission costs a link and a wrong claim hands the entity to a stranger. The YouTube and GitHub entries were dropped rather than corrected: nothing anywhere else refers to either, so there is nothing to correct them against. One test bug worth recording: the first version banned any sameAs URL ending in 'agentbio', which rejects linkedin.com/company/agentbio/ — the single entry in the old list that was actually right. The five wrong accounts are now named literally.

userStories.title: Structured data asserted two URLs the site has never had, one of them a search endpoint
userStories.description: A URL inside JSON-LD is an assertion that the URL is a thing. Two were false. ContactPoint.url named https://agentbio.net/contact on seven pages, from src/lib/seo.ts and src/components/seo/PageSEO.tsx; /contact has never been a route in App.tsx. The WebSite potentialAction named a SearchAction at /search?q={search_term_string} from three places — Landing.tsx, PageSEO.tsx and SchemaMarkup.tsx — and /search has never been a route either. SearchAction is specifically what Google reads to offer a sitelinks searchbox, so the one it would have rendered sent people to a page that does not exist. While the /* catch-all was in place both at least answered 200 with the homepage; since US-176 they are real 404s. Separately, BlogListSEO declares a SearchAction against /blog?search={search_term_string} — a claim that was equally untrue, because Blog.tsx kept its search term in useState and never read the parameter.

The blog's SearchAction becomes true: /blog reads ?search= and ?category= from the URL

The blog case is the one worth the extra work: the schema was already declaring /blog?search=, so making Blog.tsx read the parameter turned an existing false claim true rather than deleting a capability — and a filtered blog view became a link somebody can share. userStories.title: Every article was attributed to a person who does not exist

BlogArticle.tsx repeated it as a visible byline wrapped in itemProp=author itemType=schema.org/Person. userStories.title: The deployed root held two developer files, and the header rules were written for the pre-prerender site
userStories.description: Vite copies public/ into dist/ verbatim, so public/icons/generate-icons.sh and public/icons/README.md were published at https://agentbio.net/icons/generate-icons.sh and /icons/README.md — fetchable, crawlable, and not part of the site. The README opens 'This directory should contain the following PWA icon files', which is a document telling anyone who finds it that the site's icons may be missing. Same shape as US-160's source maps. Separately, public/_headers still described the site as it was before US-147 prerendered every page: its only HTML rule was `/index.html`, a path no visitor requests once each page is served from its own directory at an extensionless URL, so the Content-Type and revalidation policy it appeared to set applied to nothing. It had rules for /*.ts and /*.tsx declaring TypeScript source to be application/javascript and cacheable for a year; /*.mjs, which nothing emits; no rule for /*.webp, which ships; and its /*.js immutable rule matched /sw.js, telling caches never to revalidate the one file that controls whether a returning visitor gets an update.
acceptanceCriteria: public/ contains only files a browser requests as part of the site
No header rule types a source-code extension as executable script
Every asset type the build emits has an explicit cache policy, and the service worker is excluded from the immutable one
There is a cache policy floor that applies to the prerendered pages at their real URLs
A test enforces all of it, demonstrated failing against the state as it shipped
userStories.notes: Done 2026-09-10, iteration 12 of the SEO loop. Six of the seven checks fail on the shipped state. Two judgement calls worth recording. First, the /sw.js rule is placed AFTER /*.js rather than before: Cloudflare applies every matching rule and a later one wins for a repeated header, and a reading where the more specific path wins gives the same answer from that position — so it is correct under either, which is what you want from a rule that cannot be tested from the repository. Second, the test does not ban rules that currently match nothing: a /*.jpg rule costs nothing and is right the day an image lands. It bans rules that are wrong regardless of what matches them, which is what /*.ts was. Three things were checked and found NOT to be defects: the service worker is network-first for navigations, so it cannot serve a stale document; the pages excluded from the sitemap all carry noindex (29 in the sitemap plus 30 noindex is exactly the 59 built pages); and no indexable page is thin, duplicated or missing an h1.

userStories.title: The blog index linked to six category pages the build does not render
userStories.description: Blog.tsx rendered a 'Browse by Category' card for every entry in BLOG_CATEGORIES, all eight, regardless of whether any article carried that category. US-166 made scripts/lib/articles.mts generate a /blog/category/{slug} route only for a category that has a published article — so the page whose job is to send people into the blog spent six of its links on pages the build does not produce. Under the old `/* /index.html 200` fallback those answered with the homepage: invisible to a reader who did not check the address bar, and a duplicate of the homepage to a crawler. The heading disappears with the grid when there are none, rather than leaving an empty section
